 The Company

## We build the part that has to be right.

 § 01 / OVERVIEW 

 Rewind Dynamics is a defence-technology company headquartered in
 New Delhi. We design and develop autonomous systems that can sense their surroundings, make decisions
 and act — reducing risk to personnel and extending what a single operator can achieve.

 Our work spans three families of autonomous platforms — unmanned aerial,
 precision-guided and tactical — unified by a common core of autonomy, perception and dependable systems
 engineering. We build for real operating conditions, for defence and military users worldwide. We
 share what we're working on; the specifics we keep for the people who need them.

 Why Autonomy, Why Now

## Nobody should have to take our word for it.

 Autonomy is becoming decisive across modern
 defence. We believe the forces that depend on these systems should be able to understand, adapt and
 improve them — not treat them as sealed imports.

 Rewind Dynamics is being built in that spirit: to contribute
 trustworthy, software-first autonomous systems to defence and military users around the world,
 engineered from first principles and owned end to end.

 More about the company

 Our Approach

## The name is the method.

 We record every test, rewind 
 it, understand exactly what happened, and feed that back into the next iteration. Dependable autonomy
 is earned through disciplined engineering and honest testing — not a single demonstration.

 It is a deliberately rigorous way to build. It keeps us honest about what
 we're actually building, and it is how we intend to earn trust — with operators, partners and the
 institutions we serve.

 Who We Are  ·  Est. 2020  ·  New Delhi

## A close-knit team with a long horizon.

 We started in 2020 with a small room in New Delhi and one conviction: that the
 forces who depend on autonomous systems should be able to understand them. Six years later
 we are still small, still stubborn about that, and building for governments and armed forces
 worldwide — with a first real-world mission test coming this December.

 Our Story

## Six years of foundations, and one test ahead.

 § 01 / STORY 

 Autonomous systems are becoming important to defence around the world. We think
 the forces that rely on them deserve capability they can actually understand and own — and we
 started Rewind Dynamics to help build it.

 Our focus is the autonomy itself: the software and
 engineering that let a machine sense its surroundings, make decisions and move on its own. We're
 applying that to autonomous bodies — unmanned aerial, precision-guided and tactical platforms.

 Our name reflects how we intend to work. We record each test, rewind 
 it, understand what happened, and use that to make the next version better. Progress in autonomy comes
 from disciplined iteration.

 We've been at this since 2020, building the
 foundations deliberately — the autonomy, the team and the engineering. Our priority has been getting
 the fundamentals right rather than rushing to announce finished products.

 Mission

### Send the machine, not the person.

 To develop autonomous systems that can take on tasks which are dull, repetitive or
 dangerous — so that people can stay at a safer distance.

 Vision

### Autonomy that earns the trust placed in it.

 To become a dependable source of autonomous systems for defence and military users
 around the world — with technology that is dependable, accountable and owned end to end.

 What We Stand For

## Principles that don't bend.

 § 02 / VALUES 

 01 
### Be Useful
 Solve real problems for the people who'll use our systems. Usefulness beats novelty.

 02 
### Test Honestly
 Let real testing and data decide — not a polished demo. We'd rather find problems early.

 03 
### Iterate
 Build, test, learn, repeat. Steady, disciplined progress on hard engineering.

 04 
### Stay Accountable
 Machines carry out tasks; people set the rules and stay responsible. We design for that.

 Our Systems

## The systems we build.

 Rewind Dynamics develops three families of autonomous systems for defence and
 military applications — unmanned aerial, precision-guided and tactical. Each shares a common core of autonomy,
 perception and dependable engineering; each is shaped for a different mission.

 S-01 

## Unmanned Aerial 
 Autonomous aerial systems for surveillance, reconnaissance and force protection.

 S-02 

## Precision Guidance 
 Navigation, perception and decision software for accurate, accountable effects.

 S-03 

## Tactical Miniature 
 Compact, man-portable systems for close-range and dismounted use.

 All three families are currently
 under active research and development — nothing has been fielded, and our first real-world mission
 test is planned for December 2026 . We share the shape of what we're building here; detailed

 System 01

## Unmanned Aerial Systems

 Aircraft that fly and complete a mission with
 minimal operator workload. We develop autonomous UAVs for intelligence, surveillance and
 reconnaissance (ISR) and for force protection — systems that can watch, understand and report from
 positions we'd rather not put people in.

 Our engineering emphasis is on autonomy that
 holds up in the field: reliable navigation, useful onboard perception, and graceful behaviour when
 conditions or communications turn difficult.

 Autonomous flight & navigation Plan, fly and adjust a route with the operator supervising rather than piloting.

 Onboard perception Detect and track what matters, and report it clearly.

 Resilient by design Sensible behaviour when the link is degraded or the picture is incomplete.

 Explore unmanned aerial systems

 Unmanned Aerial ISR 

 System 02

## Precision Guidance

 Accuracy is restraint. A system that reaches
 exactly what it was directed at — and nothing else — is what makes a proportionate action possible and
 a commander genuinely accountable for it. We build the navigation, perception and decision software
 that tightens that error radius.

 Guidance is a chain: inertial navigation that
 cannot be jammed, satellite navigation that bounds its drift, and a terminal seeker that looks at the
 actual scene rather than trusting coordinates. Our contribution is the software layer across all three.

 Coupled INS/GNSS navigation Inertial and satellite navigation fused so neither one's weakness becomes the system's.

 Terminal perception Recognising the designated aimpoint in poor conditions — a perception problem first.

 Authorised by a person, always Nothing selects or engages on its own authority. Abort is always available.

 Explore precision guidance

 Precision Guidance Accuracy 
 
 Midcourse Coupled INS/GNSS navigation 

 Terminal Seeker refines onto the aimpoint 

 Measure Circular error probable (CEP) 

 Authority Human authorisation, always

 System 03

## Tactical Miniature Systems

 Small, man-portable autonomous systems for
 close-range and dismounted use. When size, weight and power are tightly limited, simplicity and
 ruggedness matter more than anything — and that constraint is exactly what we find interesting.

 The goal is capable autonomy in a package a
 soldier can carry and trust: quick to deploy, light on logistics, and dependable when it counts.

 Compact autonomy Meaningful capability on small, low-power hardware.

 Rugged & simple Built to be dependable and easy to operate under pressure.

 Rapid to deploy Minimal setup and a light logistics footprint.

 System 01  ·  Unmanned Aerial

## Unmanned aerial systems.

 Autonomous aircraft that fly a mission and report what matters, with the operator
 supervising rather than piloting. We develop UAVs for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR)
 and for force protection — systems that can watch, understand and report from positions we would rather
 not put people in.

 The Idea

## Fewer pilots. More understanding.

 § 01 / OVERVIEW 

 A conventional drone moves the pilot from the cockpit to the ground. That is
 useful, but it still consumes a trained person for every aircraft in the air. Autonomy changes the ratio:
 the aircraft handles flying, and the person handles judgement.

 Our emphasis is on the part that is genuinely hard — autonomy that holds up when
 the picture is incomplete. Reliable navigation, useful onboard perception, and sensible behaviour when
 conditions, weather or communications turn difficult. An aircraft that only works on a clear day with a
 strong link is not an aircraft you can plan around.

 What It Does

## Built around the mission, not the airframe.

 The airframe is a means to an end. What
 determines whether a UAV is useful is the software: how it plans, what it notices, and how it behaves
 when something goes wrong.

 Autonomous flight & navigation Plan, fly and adjust a route without a person on the sticks — including where satellite navigation is unreliable.

 Onboard perception Detect and track what matters in real time, on the aircraft, and report it clearly rather than dumping raw video.

 Resilient behaviour Sensible, predictable action when the link degrades, the weather turns, or the picture is incomplete.

 Operator supervision A person sets the task and can intervene at any moment — command stays human.

 Mission Roles ISR 
 
 Surveillance Persistent observation of an area 

 Reconnaissance Answering a question about a place 

 Force protection Early warning around people and sites 

 Situational picture Feeding what it sees back to command 

 Stage Research & development 

 Hard Problems

## What we're actually working on.

 The engineering that decides whether an
 autonomous aircraft is a demo or a dependable tool.

 § 02 / ENGINEERING 

 01 
### Navigation without GPS
 Satellite signals can be jammed, spoofed or simply absent. Knowing where you are using what you can see and sense is foundational, not optional.
 
 02 
### Perception that earns trust
 Detecting and tracking reliably in clutter, poor light and bad weather — and being honest about uncertainty rather than guessing confidently.
 
 03 
### Degraded-link autonomy
 Continuing the mission sensibly when the radio link thins or drops, then re-joining cleanly when it returns.
 
 04 
### Endurance vs. payload
 Every gram of sensor costs time in the air. Getting useful capability inside a strict weight and power budget is a constant trade.
 
 05 
### Safe failure
 What the aircraft does when something breaks matters more than what it does when everything works.
 
 06 
### Clean hand-off
 Handing control between autonomy and operator without confusion about who is flying.

 Anatomy

## What is actually on board.

 An unmanned aircraft is six subsystems that have to agree with each other several hundred times a second. Understanding what each one does is the fastest way to understand why autonomy is hard.

 § 03 / ANATOMY 

 01 
### Airframe & propulsion
 The physical aircraft — fixed-wing for endurance and range, rotary or hybrid for hovering and confined launch. This choice sets the mission envelope before a line of software is written: you cannot give an airframe endurance it does not have.
 02 
### Flight control system
 The autopilot. It runs the inner control loop that keeps the aircraft stable — attitude, airspeed, altitude — hundreds of times a second, and executes the outer loop that follows a route. A person supervising a mission is talking to this, not flying the aircraft.
 03 
### Inertial measurement unit
 Accelerometers and gyroscopes sensing linear acceleration and rotation rate. Integrated over time they yield attitude and position without any outside reference — unjammable, but drifting steadily, which is why they are always paired with something that corrects them.
 04 
### Navigation solution
 An attitude and heading reference fusing the IMU with satellite navigation, barometric altitude, magnetometer and airspeed. This fused estimate — not any single sensor — is what the aircraft actually believes about where it is, and it carries a confidence value with it.
 05 
### Payload & gimbal
 The reason the aircraft exists. Typically a stabilised gimbal carrying electro-optical and infrared cameras. The gimbal isolates the sensor from airframe motion so the picture stays steady while the aircraft manoeuvres.
 06 
### Datalink & ground control
 The radio link to the ground control station, where an operator sets tasking, watches the picture and intervenes. The link is assumed to be intermittent, contested and sometimes absent — which is exactly why the intelligence lives on the aircraft.

 A Mission, Start To Finish

## What actually happens.

 Stripped of jargon, an autonomous sortie runs through the same sequence every time. Most of it involves no human input at all — which is the entire point.

 Plan and upload An operator defines the objective — an area to cover, a route to follow, a point to observe — plus the limits the aircraft must not cross. This is the moment human command is exercised most concretely.

 Launch and climb The flight control system takes the aircraft off and climbs to its transit altitude on its own, holding attitude and airspeed against wind it has never seen before.

 Transit and execute The aircraft navigates to the area and executes the task, adjusting its route as wind, weather or the picture changes. Perception runs continuously on board, reporting what matters rather than streaming raw video.

 Lost link If the datalink degrades or drops, the aircraft does not stop thinking. A defined lost-link routine takes over — continue, orbit, or return to a known point where contact can be re-established — chosen in advance, never improvised.

 Recover and review The aircraft returns and lands autonomously. Every second of the sortie is recorded, replayed and assessed honestly afterwards — the discipline our name refers to.

 Sortie Sequence 
 
 Planning Operator sets task and limits 

 Launch Autonomous takeoff and climb 

 Transit Coupled INS/GNSS navigation 

 On task Onboard perception and reporting 

 Link loss Pre-defined lost-link routine 

 Recovery Autonomous return and landing 

 This system is under active research and development . Nothing described here has been fielded, and we do not publish specifications or performance figures. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026 . Detail is shared directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms — get in touch .

 Common Questions

## Questions we're actually asked.

 § 99 / FAQ 

 What is an unmanned aerial system (UAS)? A UAS is the whole system, not just the aircraft: the unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) itself, its flight control system and navigation, the payload it carries, the datalink, and the ground control station an operator works from. The term UAV usually refers to the aircraft alone.

 How does an autonomous UAV navigate without a pilot? The flight control system runs an inner loop that holds the aircraft stable — attitude, airspeed and altitude — hundreds of times a second, and an outer loop that follows a planned route. Position comes from a fused navigation solution combining an inertial measurement unit with satellite navigation, barometric altitude and airspeed. The operator sets the task and supervises; they do not fly the aircraft.

 What happens if a UAV loses its communications link? A defined lost-link routine takes over, chosen in advance rather than improvised. Depending on the mission that may mean continuing the task, orbiting in place, or returning to a known point where contact can be re-established. Because the intelligence runs on the aircraft, losing the link does not stop it thinking.

 What is ISR, and how do UAVs support it? ISR stands for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance — finding out what is happening somewhere so decisions rest on fact. Autonomous UAVs help because they do not lose attention over long uneventful periods, and they can report conclusions rather than streaming raw video for a person to review.

 Are Rewind Dynamics UAVs in service? No. All our systems are under active research and development. Nothing has been fielded, and our first end-to-end real-world mission test is planned for December 2026.

 System 02  ·  Precision Guidance

## Precision guidance.

 Accuracy is a humanitarian technology as much as a military one. A system that reaches exactly what it was directed at, and nothing else, is the difference between a proportionate action and an indiscriminate one. That is the engineering problem we work on.

 The Case For Precision

## Accuracy is restraint.

 § 01 / RATIONALE 

 Before guidance, hitting one specific point meant delivering a great many unguided munitions and accepting whatever else was within the error radius. Precision inverted that arithmetic: fewer effects, smaller warheads, less collateral damage, and a far greater chance that what was intended is what actually happens.

 This is why we regard precision as an accountability technology. A commander can only be answerable for an outcome they could reasonably predict. Tightening the error radius is what makes prediction — and therefore responsibility — possible. Our work here is guidance and accountability engineering; a person authorises every action, always.

 How Guidance Works

## The accuracy chain.

 Guidance is not one technology but a chain of them, each covering the phase where the others are weakest. These are the publicly understood principles the field is built on.

 § 02 / PRINCIPLES 

 01 
### Inertial navigation (INS)
 An inertial measurement unit senses acceleration and rotation and integrates them into a position estimate. It needs nothing from the outside world — which makes it unjammable — but its error grows steadily with time, so it cannot work alone over long flights.
 02 
### Satellite navigation (GNSS)
 A satellite fix corrects inertial drift and holds accuracy roughly constant over distance. The weakness is the opposite of the INS: the signal is weak, and can be jammed or spoofed by an adversary.
 03 
### Coupled INS/GNSS
 Fusing the two covers both weaknesses. Satellite fixes bound the inertial drift; the inertial solution carries the system honestly through periods when satellite navigation is unavailable or untrustworthy.
 04 
### Midcourse guidance
 The long phase where the system travels toward the area of interest, flying a planned trajectory on the coupled navigation solution and updating it as conditions change.
 05 
### Terminal guidance
 The final phase, where a seeker looks at the actual scene and refines aim onto the specific designated point rather than a set of coordinates — the step that separates good accuracy from precision.
 06 
### Circular error probable (CEP)
 The standard measure: the radius within which half of all deliveries fall. Every element of the chain contributes error, and the total is what CEP expresses.

 Terminal Seekers

## Looking at the scene, not the coordinates.

 Coordinates can be slightly wrong, and things move. A terminal seeker resolves that by sensing the actual scene in the final phase. Each seeker type trades differently between weather, cost and the kind of designation required.

 Semi-active laser Homes on laser energy reflected from a point designated by an operator or an aircraft. Very precise, and it keeps a human explicitly in the loop — someone must actively designate.

 Imaging infrared Forms a thermal image and matches it against the intended aimpoint. Works at night and needs no external designation, at higher cost and with some weather sensitivity.

 Millimetre-wave radar Sees through cloud, dust, smoke and rain where optical seekers struggle — the all-weather option in the family.

 Multi-mode Combining seekers so that the failure conditions of one are covered by another, which is the direction most modern work takes.

 Guidance Chain Phases 
 
 Launch Alignment and handover 

 Midcourse Coupled INS/GNSS navigation 

 Terminal Seeker refines onto the aimpoint 

 Measure Circular error probable (CEP) 

 Authority Human authorisation, always 

 Stage Research & development 

 Our Work

## Where we contribute.

 We are an autonomy and guidance software company. Our contribution is the navigation, perception and decision layer — the same core that runs our unmanned aerial and tactical systems — applied to the accuracy chain.

 Navigation that survives denial Guidance is only as good as its position estimate. Our GPS-denied navigation work applies directly here.

 Perception for terminal phases Recognising the designated aimpoint reliably, in poor conditions, is a perception problem before it is anything else.

 Honest uncertainty A guidance system that knows how confident it should be can abort rather than proceed on a bad solution. We treat that as a required feature.

 Abort and authority The ability to withhold, redirect or abort is designed in from the start, not added afterwards.

 Our Contribution Software 
 
 We build Navigation, perception, decision software 

 Applied to The accuracy chain 

 Shared with UAV and tactical programmes 

 Constraint Human authorises every action 

 Stage Research & development 

 Non-Negotiables

## Limits we design in.

 These are constraints on what we will build, not options a customer can configure away.

 § 03 / LIMITS 

 01 
### A person authorises
 No system we build selects and engages on its own authority. Authorisation is human, explicitly and always.

 02 
### Abort is always available
 The ability to stop or redirect is a first-class requirement, not a fallback.

 03 
### Refuse on low confidence
 A system unsure of its solution should decline rather than proceed.

 04 
### Reconstructable afterwards
 Every decision recorded so an action can be examined and accounted for.

 This page explains publicly documented guidance principles at a conceptual level. We do not publish designs, parameters, performance figures or any implementation detail.  All Systems 

 Common Questions

## Questions we're actually asked.

 § 99 / FAQ 

 What is a precision-guided system? A system that uses guidance to reach a specific designated point with a far smaller margin of error than an unguided equivalent. That margin is normally expressed as circular error probable, or CEP — the radius within which half of all deliveries fall.

 Why combine inertial and satellite navigation? They fail in opposite ways. An inertial measurement unit needs nothing from outside and cannot be jammed, but its error grows steadily with time. Satellite navigation holds accuracy roughly constant but the signal is weak and can be jammed or spoofed. Coupled together, satellite fixes bound the inertial drift and the inertial solution carries the system honestly through periods when satellite navigation cannot be trusted.

 What is terminal guidance? The final phase, where a seeker senses the actual scene rather than trusting coordinates. Common approaches include semi-active laser, which homes on energy reflected from a point a person actively designates; imaging infrared, which matches a thermal image; and millimetre-wave radar, which works through cloud, dust and smoke.

 Does Rewind Dynamics build autonomous weapons? No. A person authorises every consequential action. We do not build systems that select and engage on their own authority, abort is always available, and a system unsure of its solution is designed to decline rather than proceed. This is a limit on what we will build, not a setting a customer can change.

 Do you publish specifications or performance figures? No. We explain publicly documented guidance principles at a conceptual level only. Designs, parameters and performance figures are never published, and technical material is shared with government programmes and evaluators only after end-use and end-user assessment.

 System 03  ·  Tactical Miniature

## Tactical miniature systems.

 Small, man-portable autonomous systems for close-range and dismounted use. When
 size, weight and power are tightly limited, simplicity and ruggedness matter more than anything — and that
 constraint is exactly what makes the problem interesting.

 The Idea

## Capability you can carry.

 § 01 / OVERVIEW 

 The tactical edge is where most decisions actually get made — close,
 cluttered, and often without a reliable link to anyone else. A system that helps there has to be small
 enough to carry, quick enough to deploy, and self-sufficient enough to work without a support chain.

 That is a brutal engineering constraint, and a clarifying one. Every gram and
 every watt has to justify itself. What survives the cut tends to be the capability that genuinely
 matters: see a bit further, understand a bit more, and do it without adding to what someone already
 has to carry.

 Design Principles

## Small, rugged, and honest about limits.

 A tactical system earns its place by being
 dependable and unobtrusive. If it needs babysitting, it is a liability rather than an asset.

 Compact autonomy Meaningful capability running on small, low-power hardware — the intelligence lives on the device.

 Fast to deploy Usable within moments by someone who has other things to worry about.

 Light on logistics Minimal support, minimal setup, minimal training overhead.

 Works alone Continues to be useful without a constant link back to anyone.

 Constraints SWaP 
 
 Size Man-portable by design 

 Weight Carried alongside existing kit 

 Power Strict on-board energy budget 

 Link Assumed intermittent or absent 

 Stage Research & development 

 Why It's Hard

## Everything is a trade-off.

 Miniature systems remove every comfortable
 assumption you get to make on a larger platform.

 § 02 / ENGINEERING 

 01 
### Compute in a matchbox
 Running capable perception and autonomy on hardware with a fraction of the power a larger platform can spare.
 
 02 
### Energy is everything
 Endurance, compute and sensing all draw from the same small battery. Every choice costs another.
 
 03 
### Ruggedness
 Small things get dropped, knocked and rained on. Surviving ordinary handling is a hard requirement.
 
 04 
### Simplicity under stress
 The interface has to make sense to someone who is tired, busy and not thinking about your product.

 This system is under active research and development . Nothing described here has been fielded, and we do not publish specifications or performance figures. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026 . Detail is shared directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms — get in touch .

## Capability areas.

 Autonomy isn't one thing — it's several fields working together, from the sensors
 that take in the world to the software that decides what to do. These are the areas we focus on. For a
 plainer, general explanation of the technology, see our Technology page.

 Domain 01

## Autonomy Core

 The decision-making part of a system —
 how it plans a task, adapts as things change, and controls its own movement with limited human
 input. This is the core of what we work on.

 Planning Working out routes and actions, and adjusting them as the situation changes.

 Navigation Knowing where it is and finding its way, including when signals are unreliable.

 Bounded behaviour Operating inside clear limits, with actions that can be reviewed afterwards.

 Common Questions

## Straight answers.

 Do you build the systems or just the software? Our main focus is the autonomy — the software and engineering that make a system autonomous — and we're applying it to autonomous bodies (unmanned aerial, precision-guided and tactical). We're at an early, development stage.

 Why run the intelligence on the device? Doing the computing on board (rather than in the cloud) means a system can keep working without a constant network connection, and its data can stay on the device. It's a sensible default for defence use.

 How do you think about accountability? Our view is simple: machines can carry out tasks, but people set the rules and stay responsible. We design systems so a person can supervise, and so decisions can be reviewed afterwards.

 Can we see specifications or a product? We're not publishing specifications or claiming a finished product at this stage. If you're a partner, supplier or program and want to talk, please get in touch .

 Capability 01  ·  Autonomy

## Autonomy.

 Autonomy is the part that decides. Given a goal and a picture of the world, it works out what to do next — and keeps working it out as the situation changes. It is the difference between a remote-controlled machine and a system that genuinely reduces workload.

 What It Means

## Not one thing, but a spectrum.

 § 01 / DEFINITION 

 Autonomy is often talked about as a switch — either a machine is autonomous or it isn't. In practice it is a spectrum, and the useful question is always autonomous at what? A platform might navigate a route entirely on its own while still requiring a person to approve anything consequential.

 We design deliberately along that spectrum. The goal is not to remove people; it is to remove the parts of the job that consume attention without needing judgement — holding a heading, flying a search pattern, watching a feed for hours — so the person can spend their attention on the things that actually need a human.

 Inside The Capability

## From goal to action.

 The autonomy layer sits above perception and below the mission. It takes in what the platform understands about the world and turns a stated objective into a sequence of concrete actions.

 Mission reasoning Turning a high-level objective — cover this area, follow this route, watch this point — into an executable plan.

 Planning & replanning Choosing a course of action, then revising it when the world turns out differently from the plan.

 Behaviour arbitration Deciding what matters most right now when several objectives compete for the same platform.

 Bounded discretion Operating freely inside limits a person has set, and stopping at the edge of them.

 Autonomy Layer Decisions 
 
 Input Mission goal + world model 

 Output Actions the platform executes 

 Runs Continuously, many times a second 

 Bounded by Operator-set rules and limits 

 Stage Research & development 

 Hard Parts

## What makes autonomy difficult.

 Anyone can make a machine follow waypoints on a clear day. Autonomy earns its name in the cases that are not clean.

 § 02 / CHALLENGES 

 01 
### Acting under uncertainty
 The world model is never complete or perfectly correct. Good autonomy behaves sensibly anyway, and knows how confident it should be.
 02 
### Knowing when to stop
 Recognising that a situation has moved outside what the system should handle alone, and handing back to a person cleanly.
 03 
### Predictability
 A system that is brilliant but unpredictable is unusable. Operators need to be able to anticipate what it will do.
 04 
### Graceful degradation
 Losing a sensor or a link should reduce capability, not produce nonsense.
 05 
### Explaining itself
 Recording enough about a decision that it can be reconstructed and understood afterwards.
 06 
### Real-time budgets
 Every decision competes for the same limited onboard compute, and the loop cannot be allowed to slow down.

 Everything described here is under active research and development . Nothing has been fielded, and we do not publish specifications or performance figures. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026 . Technical detail is shared directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms — get in touch .

 The sense–decide–act loop and the layered stack autonomy sits in.

 The limits, oversight and accountability wrapped around every decision.

 Reference  ·  Levels of Autonomy

## How autonomous is autonomous?

 "Fully autonomous" is the least useful phrase in this field. Autonomy is not a single number that a system either reaches or does not — it is a description of what a system can handle, in what conditions, with how much help. Getting that description right is the difference between a specification and a slogan.

 The Problem With Levels

## One number hides the whole question.

 § 01 / PROBLEM 

 Ask how autonomous a system is and you will usually get a level between one and ten. The trouble is that a platform which can fly a pre-planned route over open ground in clear weather with no opposition, and a platform which can pursue an objective through cluttered terrain with its satellite navigation jammed, might be assigned the same number — because the number is answering different questions in each case.

 A useful answer has to say autonomous at what, and under what conditions . That is precisely the gap the NIST ALFUS framework — Autonomy Levels for Unmanned Systems — was created to close, by giving requirements and evaluation a shared vocabulary instead of a marketing adjective.

 The Three Axes

## Autonomy has three dimensions.

 ALFUS describes autonomy as a point in a three-axis space rather than a rung on a ladder. Move along any axis and the difficulty changes, even if the platform does not.

 § 02 / AXES 

 01 
### Mission complexity
 How hard the task itself is. Holding a fixed orbit is not the same problem as searching an area, adapting to what is found, and re-planning against a changing objective. The same aircraft can be highly autonomous at one and useless at the other.
 02 
### Environmental difficulty
 What the world is doing to the system. Open sky in daylight with a strong satellite fix is the easy end. Cluttered terrain, degraded weather, jammed or spoofed navigation and an intermittent datalink is the other, and it is where real operations live.
 03 
### Human independence
 How much operator involvement is required, and of what kind. Continuous manual control sits at one extreme; a person setting an objective and boundaries and then supervising sits near the other. This axis is a design choice, not only a capability.
 04 
### Why all three matter
 A claim on any single axis is close to meaningless without the other two. High human independence in a trivially easy environment on a trivially simple mission is not an achievement — and it is exactly what a demonstration video usually shows.

 How We Specify It

## What we state, and what we won't.

 We describe our systems along these axes rather than claiming a level, because a level invites the reader to assume the other two axes were hard. Ours are still in research and development, and we would rather be precise than impressive.

 Task, stated explicitly We name the mission the autonomy handles rather than implying it generalises to every mission.

 Conditions, stated explicitly Including the degraded cases: poor light and weather, denied satellite navigation, a thinning datalink.

 Operator role, stated explicitly What the person sets, what they see, when they are asked, and how they intervene.

 Where it stops The point at which the system should hand back rather than continue — the most important number in the specification and the one least often published.

 Specifying Autonomy Three Axes 
 
 Axis 1 Mission complexity 

 Axis 2 Environmental difficulty 

 Axis 3 Human independence 

 We publish The description, not a level 

 Command Human, in all cases 

 Stage Research & development 

 Our Position

## Where we sit deliberately.

 We do not build toward maximum human independence. We build toward the point where autonomy removes workload without removing judgement.

 § 03 / POSITION 

 01 
### Attention, not authority
 Autonomy should absorb the parts of a job that consume attention without needing judgement — holding a pattern, watching a feed — and hand the rest to a person.

 02 
### Bounded discretion
 Freedom inside limits a person has set, and a stop at the edge of them rather than an improvisation past it.

 03 
### Knowing when to stop
 Recognising that a situation has left the envelope the system should handle alone is itself a capability, and we treat it as a requirement.

 04 
### Never the last word
 No system we build selects and engages on its own authority, at any point on any axis.

 The ALFUS framework is published by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology; this page summarises its structure to explain how we describe our own systems and does not imply any NIST endorsement, assessment or certification. All Rewind Dynamics systems remain under active research and development .

 Capability 02  ·  Perception

## Perception.

 Perception is how a machine finds out what is around it. Cameras and sensors produce enormous amounts of raw data; perception turns that into something a system can actually act on — what is there, where it is, and whether it matters.

 The Job

## Data is not understanding.

 § 01 / OVERVIEW 

 A camera produces pixels. A sensor produces numbers. Neither is knowledge. Perception is the work of converting that raw stream into a structured picture — objects, positions, movement — at a rate fast enough to act on and with reliability you can plan around.

 This is where most autonomy projects quietly fail. A perception stack that works on clean daytime footage and falls apart in rain, dust, glare or low light is not a capability; it is a demonstration. We care much more about the difficult end of that range than the easy end.

 How It Works

## One picture from many sources.

 No single sensor is good at everything. Cameras see detail but struggle in darkness; other sensors work in conditions cameras cannot. Fusing them produces something more dependable than any one alone.

 Detection Finding the things in a scene that are worth paying attention to.

 Tracking Following those things over time, so the system understands movement rather than isolated snapshots.

 Sensor fusion Combining several sensors into a single, coherent picture — including resolving disagreements between them.

 Uncertainty Attaching honest confidence to what is reported, so downstream decisions can account for doubt.

 Perception Stack Real-Time 
 
 Input Camera and sensor streams 

 Output Structured world model 

 Runs On the platform, in real time 

 Designed for Clutter, poor light, bad weather 

 Stage Research & development 

 What We Optimise For

## Reliable beats impressive.

 The metrics that matter for a defence system are not the ones that make for a good demo video.

 § 02 / PRIORITIES 

 01 
### False alarms
 A system that cries wolf gets switched off. Precision matters as much as raw detection rate.
 02 
### Degraded conditions
 Night, rain, dust, glare, smoke and motion blur are the normal case, not the exception.
 03 
### Small and distant objects
 The things worth seeing are usually far away and occupy very few pixels.
 04 
### Compute cost
 Perception has to fit in the same power budget as everything else on the platform.
 05 
### Honest confidence
 Reporting uncertainty properly is more useful than a confident guess.
 06 
### Consistency over time
 Stable tracking matters more than a perfect single frame.

 Everything described here is under active research and development . Nothing has been fielded, and we do not publish specifications or performance figures. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026 . Technical detail is shared directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms — get in touch .

### Autonomy
 What the system does with the picture perception produces.

### Navigation
 Using what the system sees to work out where it is.

Multi-Sensor Fusion Explained | Rewind Dynamics 

 Skip to content

 Capability  ·  Sensor Fusion

## No single sensor sees everything.

 Every sensing method has a condition that defeats it. Fusion is not about adding sensors until the problem goes away — it is about combining methods whose failure modes do not overlap, and being honest about what the combination still cannot see.

 The Principle

## Complementary failure, not redundancy.

 § 01 / PRINCIPLE 

 Adding a second sensor of the same kind gives you a little more confidence and the same blind spots. Adding a sensor that fails differently gives you coverage. That distinction is the whole discipline: you are not buying redundancy, you are buying complementary failure modes.

 The small uncrewed aircraft problem illustrates it well, because it defeats each modality in a different way. Understanding why is the fastest route to understanding why fusion is necessary rather than merely nice.

 The Modalities

## What each sensor is good and bad at.

 Four sensing methods, each with a genuine advantage and a genuine defeat condition. The trade-offs below are well documented in the open literature.

 § 02 / MODALITIES 

 01 
### Radar
 The only modality that yields range, bearing, altitude and radial speed simultaneously, and it works in weather and darkness. Against small aircraft it struggles: a low radar cross-section, and ground clutter at low grazing angles that a slow, low target hides inside.
 02 
### Radio frequency
 Passive interception of the command-and-control link, which can identify and often locate the operator as well as the aircraft. Its defeat condition is decisive and increasingly common: an autonomous platform that radiates little or nothing gives an RF sensor nothing to hear .
 03 
### Electro-optical / infrared
 Produces imagery a human can immediately interpret and confirm, which matters when a decision follows. It requires unobstructed line of sight and adequate illumination or thermal contrast, so cloud, dust, smoke and obscuration degrade it sharply.
 04 
### Acoustic
 Fully passive, transmitting nothing, and propeller harmonics are distinctive enough to separate an aircraft from a bird. The range is short, ambient noise interferes, and individual aircraft within a group are hard to separate.
 05 
### Micro-Doppler
 Rotating blades modulate a radar return in a way the airframe alone does not, producing a signature that helps classify what has been detected rather than merely noticing it. The signature weakens with distance and with smaller rotors, exactly where you most want it.
 06 
### The gap that remains
 A small, autonomous, radio-silent aircraft flying low against clutter in poor visibility is difficult for every modality at once. Any vendor claiming otherwise is describing a demonstration, not a capability.

 Making One Picture

## From four opinions to one track.

 Fusion happens after detection, and it is where most of the engineering difficulty actually sits. Four sensors will disagree — about how many objects exist, where they are, and what they are — and something has to resolve that into a single picture a person can act on.

 Association Deciding which detections from different sensors belong to the same object. Get this wrong and one aircraft becomes three tracks, or three become one.

 Cross-cueing Letting one sensor point another. A radar contact can slew a camera onto a bearing far faster than a human could, turning a detection into a visual confirmation.

 Weighting by trust Each sensor's contribution weighted by how much it can be trusted in the present conditions, not by a fixed constant. A camera at night and a camera at noon are different sensors.

 Track continuity Holding an object's identity as it manoeuvres, is briefly occluded, or passes between sensors' coverage — so the operator sees one continuous thing, not a series of unrelated blips.

 Honest uncertainty Every fused output carries a confidence. A system that reports certainty it has not earned is more dangerous than one that reports doubt.

 Fusion Pipeline 
 
 Input Independent sensor detections 

 Associate Which detections are one object 

 Cross-cue One sensor points another 

 Weight By present, not nominal, reliability 

 Output One track picture with confidence 

 Decision Made by a person 

 Why This Is Our Problem

## Fusion is software.

 The sensors are largely commodity. What separates a useful system from a pile of hardware is the layer that reconciles them — and that is where we work.

 § 03 / OUR WORK 

 01 
### It travels across programmes
 The same fusion core serves ISR, force protection and counter-UAS. An improvement made for one reaches all three.

 02 
### It runs on the platform
 Fusion has to complete inside the same power and thermal budget as everything else on board. See edge AI .

 03 
### It decides what to send
 There is rarely enough bandwidth for raw feeds, so fusion also decides what is worth transmitting.

 04 
### It is where trust is won or lost
 False alarms come from bad fusion more often than from bad sensors, and a system that cries wolf is switched off.

 This page summarises publicly documented sensing principles to explain our approach. It describes no product, and we publish no specifications, detection ranges or performance figures. All work is under active research and development .

 Fusing inertial and satellite navigation on the same principle.

 Capability 03  ·  Edge AI

## Edge AI.

 Edge AI means the intelligence runs on the platform itself, not in a data centre somewhere. For defence autonomy this is not an optimisation or a preference — it is a requirement, and it shapes every engineering decision we make.

 Why Not The Cloud

## A link you cannot rely on is not a link.

 § 01 / RATIONALE 

 Cloud inference assumes a fast, reliable, permanently available connection. In defence, that assumption fails routinely — links are contested, jammed, saturated or simply out of range. A system that stops thinking when the radio drops is not a system anyone can plan a mission around.

 There are three further reasons beyond availability. Latency: a control loop that has to wait for a round trip is too slow to matter. Bandwidth: sending raw sensor data off-platform is wasteful and often impossible. And security: the less that has to leave the platform, the smaller the surface you have to defend.

 The Engineering

## Capable models, tiny budgets.

 The hard part is not deciding to run at the edge; it is making capable intelligence fit. Onboard compute is limited by weight, heat and power, and every watt spent thinking is a watt not spent moving.

 Model efficiency Designing and compressing models so they run usefully within a strict compute envelope.

 Deterministic timing Guaranteeing the loop completes on schedule, every time, rather than usually.

 Thermal & power budget Sustained performance without overheating or draining endurance.

 Graceful degradation Shedding non-essential work under load instead of falling over.

 Edge Compute On-Platform 
 
 Runs Entirely on the platform 

 Assumes No reliable link 

 Constraint Size, weight and power 

 Priority Deterministic real-time behaviour 

 Stage Research & development 

 The Payoff

## What edge buys you.

 § 02 / BENEFITS 

 01 
### Independence
 The platform stays useful when it is alone, which is when it matters most.

 02 
### Speed
 Decisions happen at sensor rate, not at network rate.

 03 
### Lower exposure
 Less data leaving the platform means a smaller attack surface.

 04 
### Bandwidth for what counts
 Send conclusions, not raw video.

 Everything described here is under active research and development . Nothing has been fielded, and we do not publish specifications or performance figures. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026 . Technical detail is shared directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms — get in touch .

 If you work on efficient models, embedded compute or real-time systems, we'd like to talk.

 Capability 04  ·  Navigation

## Navigation in denied conditions.

 Knowing where you are sounds like a solved problem — until satellite navigation is jammed, spoofed or simply unavailable. For a defence system, assuming GPS will be there is a design flaw. We treat its absence as the normal case.

 The Problem

## Satellite positioning is the first thing to go.

 § 01 / PROBLEM 

 Global navigation satellite systems broadcast a very weak signal from a very long way away. That makes them straightforward to jam and, more concerning, to spoof — feeding a receiver a plausible but wrong position. A platform that silently believes a false position is more dangerous than one that knows it is lost.

 So we build navigation that degrades honestly. When satellite positioning is unavailable or untrustworthy, the system should keep functioning using what it can see and sense directly — and it should know how much confidence to place in its own estimate.

 The Approach

## Position from first principles.

 There is no single replacement for satellite navigation. What works is combining several independent methods, each with different failure modes, into one estimate that is more robust than any of them alone.

 Visual odometry Estimating movement by tracking how the world shifts across the camera between frames.

 Mapping & relocalisation Building a map of the surroundings while working out your position within it, and recognising places already seen.

 Inertial dead reckoning Using motion sensors to carry the estimate forward through gaps — accurate over short intervals, drifting over long ones.

 Fused estimation Weighting every source by how much it can currently be trusted, and flagging when the estimate is degrading.

 Navigation GPS-Denied 
 
 Assumes Satellite positioning unavailable 

 Primary sources Vision and inertial sensing 

 Key property Honest confidence estimate 

 Failure mode Degrade, never silently drift 

 Stage Research & development 

 Why It's Hard

## The failure modes that matter.

 Navigation errors compound. A small mistake early becomes a large one later, which is why the discipline is mostly about managing error rather than eliminating it.

 § 02 / CHALLENGES 

 01 
### Drift
 Every dead-reckoned estimate accumulates error over time. The question is how fast, and how you correct it.
 02 
### Featureless environments
 Open water, desert, snow and darkness give vision very little to work with.
 03 
### Spoofing
 A false satellite fix is worse than none, because the system does not know it is wrong. Detecting that is its own problem.
 04 
### Repetitive scenes
 Places that look identical to each other cause confident relocalisation to the wrong one.
 05 
### Compute cost
 Vision-based navigation is expensive, and it competes with perception for the same hardware.
 06 
### Knowing you're lost
 Recognising that the estimate has degraded past usefulness — and saying so — is a feature, not a failure.

 Everything described here is under active research and development . Nothing has been fielded, and we do not publish specifications or performance figures. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026 . Technical detail is shared directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms — get in touch .

 Explore Further

 The vision stack that navigation draws on.

 Where GPS-denied navigation matters most for us today.

 GNSS, SLAM, dead reckoning and the rest, defined plainly.

 Capability 05  ·  Systems Engineering

## Systems engineering.

 Clever autonomy that only works in a lab is worth nothing. Systems engineering is the discipline that turns software, sensors, compute and structure into one machine that behaves the same way on a bad day as it did on the bench.

 Why It Decides Everything

## The unglamorous work that makes it real.

 § 01 / RATIONALE 

 Most of the distance between a promising prototype and a dependable system is not algorithmic. It is integration, power, thermal behaviour, vibration, connectors, timing, configuration management and test. These are the things that decide whether a platform works in the field.

 We treat this as a first-class engineering discipline rather than an afterthought at the end of development. Building it in from the start is considerably cheaper than discovering it during trials.

 What It Covers

## From bench to field.

 Systems engineering is the connective tissue: making sure that each subsystem is sound, that the interfaces between them are defined, and that the whole behaves predictably.

 Integration Bringing autonomy, sensors, compute, power and structure together as one coherent machine.

 Reliability & environment Vibration, temperature, dust, moisture and the ordinary abuse of real use.

 Verification & test Establishing that the system does what it is specified to do — repeatably, not once.

 Configuration control Knowing exactly which software and hardware are in any given unit, and being able to reproduce it.

 Discipline End-To-End 
 
 Spans Software, hardware, power, structure 

 Concerned with Interfaces and whole-system behaviour 

 Method Simulation-first, then hardware 

 Records Every run, for honest assessment 

 Stage Research & development 

 How We Work

## Principles we hold to.

 § 02 / PRINCIPLES 

 01 
### Design for test
 If a behaviour cannot be tested repeatably, it cannot be trusted.

 02 
### Fail predictably
 Define what happens when something breaks, before it breaks.

 03 
### Record everything
 Every run is captured so it can be rewound, reviewed and learned from.

 04 
### Modularity
 Clean interfaces so a subsystem can be improved without destabilising the rest.

 Everything described here is under active research and development . Nothing has been fielded, and we do not publish specifications or performance figures. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026 . Technical detail is shared directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms — get in touch .

 How It Works

## Our autonomy architecture.

 A clear look at how our systems are built to think and act — the loop they run,
 the layers that make them work, and the discipline behind them. We keep the specifics for our partners;
 the approach we're glad to share.

 The Core Loop

## Sense · Decide · Act.

 Every one of our systems runs the same loop, many
 times a second: take in the world, decide what to do, and act — then do it again. Getting that loop
 fast, reliable and safe is the heart of the work.

 § 01 / LOOP 

 01 
### Sense
 Cameras and sensors gather information about the surroundings.

 02 
### Understand
 That data is fused into a dependable picture the system can act on.

 03 
### Decide
 The autonomy core chooses an action from the mission and the situation.

 04 
### Act
 The platform moves or responds — safely, in real time — and the loop repeats.

 Architecture

## A layered, modular stack.

 We build the autonomy as clean, separable
 layers. Each can be tested and improved on its own — and because the layers are shared, an
 improvement made for one platform can benefit the others.

 Modularity also means our systems are built to integrate, not to lock
 anyone in — designed to fit alongside existing platforms and command arrangements.

 The Stack Layers 
 
 05 · Mission Goals, tasking and oversight 

 04 · Autonomy Planning, decisions, behaviour 

 03 · Perception Sensing, fusion, understanding 

 02 · Platform Guidance, navigation, control 

 01 · Compute Secure on-board hardware & runtime 

 The Building Blocks

## What goes into the autonomy.

 In plain terms, these are the parts that work
 together to make a platform autonomous. We engineer each of them, and how they fit.

 § 02 / BLOCKS 

 01 
### Navigation
 Knowing where the system is and finding its way — including when satellite signals are unreliable.

 02 
### Perception
 Turning camera and sensor data into a clear, trustworthy view of what's around the system.

 03 
### Sensor Fusion
 Combining several sensors into one picture that's more reliable than any single one alone.

 04 
### Planning
 Working out a sensible course of action, and re-planning as the situation changes.

 05 
### Control
 Keeping the platform stable and making it do precisely what's asked — steering, flight, balance.

 06 
### Edge AI
 Running the intelligence on the platform itself, so it stays effective without a constant link.

 How We Develop

## Prove it in software first.

 Much of our progress happens in simulation.
 Testing ideas in software is faster, safer and cheaper than testing them in the field — so we catch
 problems on screen, then move to hardware once the software is sound.

 Simulate Try things in software and repeat them as often as needed.

 Test on hardware Move to real devices once the software holds up.

 Record & assess Keep records of every run and assess them honestly — what went right, what went wrong — the idea behind our name.

 Test · Record · Review Method 

 Responsibility

## People stay in command.

 Autonomy should be dependable and accountable.
 Machines carry out tasks; people set the rules and stay responsible. We build for supervision,
 safety and review from the very first line of code.

 § 03 / TRUST 

 01 
### Human Oversight
 Designed so a person can supervise and step in at any time.

 02 
### Safety First
 Clear limits and safe behaviour built in, not bolted on.

 03 
### Security
 Sound security engineering as a default across the stack.

 04 
### Reviewable
 Records kept so decisions can be understood after the fact.

 05 
### Assessment
 After every run we assess honestly — what went right, what went wrong, and why — and act on it.

 We share more with partners and evaluators under appropriate terms. Reach out.

 Method  ·  Simulation & Test

## Simulation and test.

 Most of our progress happens in software. Testing an idea in simulation is faster, safer and repeatable in a way that field testing never is — so we find problems on screen, and only move to hardware once the software holds up.

 The Method

## Prove it in software first.

 § 01 / APPROACH 

 Autonomy is developed by iteration, and iteration speed decides how good a system eventually becomes. In the field, a single test can take a day to set up and produce one noisy result. In simulation, the same scenario can be run thousands of times before lunch, with every variable controlled.

 That does not make simulation a substitute for reality — it makes it the filter. By the time something reaches hardware, the obvious failures are gone, and the tests that remain are the ones that genuinely need the physical world.

 The Loop

## Test. Rewind. Assess. Improve.

 Our name describes the method. Every run — simulated or physical — is recorded, replayed and assessed honestly. What went right, what went wrong, and why.

 Simulate Run the scenario in software, as many times and as many ways as needed.

 Test on hardware Move to real devices once the behaviour holds up in software.

 Record Capture everything, so a run can be reconstructed exactly rather than remembered.

 Assess honestly Review what actually happened without flattering the result, then feed it back in.

 Development Test · Record · Review 
 
 Primary environment Simulation 

 Hardware Once software is sound 

 Every run Recorded and reviewable 

 First mission test Planned December 2026 

 Stage Research & development 

 What We Test For

## The cases that actually matter.

 Anything can be made to work in the nominal case. We spend our time on everything else.

 § 02 / SCENARIOS 

 01 
### Degraded sensing
 Poor light, weather, occlusion, and sensors that partially fail.
 02 
### Lost communications
 What the platform does when the link thins, drops, or returns unexpectedly.
 03 
### Unexpected world
 Situations the system was not explicitly designed for, to see how it fails.
 04 
### Edge of the envelope
 Behaviour right at the boundary of the limits an operator has set.
 05 
### Repeatability
 Whether the same input reliably produces the same behaviour.
 06 
### Hand-off
 Transferring control between autonomy and operator without confusion.

 Our systems have not been fielded . Everything to date has lived in development and simulation; our first end-to-end real-world mission test is planned for December 2026 . We would rather say that plainly than imply more.

 Applications

## Where autonomy earns its place.

 Our three platform families exist to serve a small number of jobs that genuinely benefit from autonomy — jobs that are dull, dangerous, or simply beyond what a small team can sustain by hand. These are the application areas we build toward.

 The Principle

## Start with the job, not the machine.

 § 01 / APPROACH 

 It is easy to build an impressive platform that answers no particular question. We work the other way round: identify a task where a person is currently exposed to risk, or where attention is the limiting factor, and ask whether autonomy meaningfully changes it.

 Every application below shares the same underlying core — autonomy, perception, edge intelligence and dependable engineering. That is deliberate. Improving the core improves every application at once, which is why we invest there rather than in bespoke one-off systems.

 Application Areas

## Four areas we build for.

 Each links through to a fuller description of the problem and how autonomy applies to it.

 § 02 / AREAS 

 01 
### Intelligence, surveillance & reconnaissance 
 Persistent observation and answering questions about a place — the largest and most immediate application of autonomy. Read more → 
 02 
### Force protection 
 Early warning and continuous watch around people, convoys and fixed sites, without tying up the people being protected. Read more → 
 03 
### Counter-UAS 
 Detecting, tracking and identifying small uncrewed aircraft — a defensive problem that has grown very quickly. Read more → 
 04 
### Tactical edge support 
 Extending what a small dismounted team can see and understand, with equipment they can actually carry. Read more → 

 Common Thread

## What these share.

 § 03 / COMMON 

 01 
### Risk moved off people
 In each case the machine goes where a person would otherwise have to.

 02 
### Attention multiplied
 One operator supervising several systems rather than driving one.

 03 
### Works when alone
 Useful without a constant communications link back.

 04 
### Human decides
 The system reports and recommends; a person judges and acts.

 Everything described here is under active research and development . Nothing has been fielded, and we do not publish specifications or performance figures. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026 . Technical detail is shared directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms — get in touch .

 Our Systems 

 Common Questions

## Questions we're actually asked.

 § 99 / FAQ 

 What defence applications does Rewind Dynamics build for? Four areas: intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR); force protection; counter-UAS, meaning the detection, tracking and identification of small uncrewed aircraft; and support at the tactical edge for small dismounted teams.

 Why is counter-UAS considered an economics problem? Because a small uncrewed aircraft can be produced very cheaply while the established means of countering one can cost orders of magnitude more. A defender can win every engagement and still lose the exchange. Our work concentrates on the sensing half — detecting, tracking and identifying reliably enough to be trusted.

 Who does Rewind Dynamics work with? Governments, armed forces, defence programmes, primes and integrators, component suppliers and research institutions — worldwide, subject to sanctions screening, export-control obligations and end-use assessment.

 Application 01  ·  ISR

## Intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance.

 ISR is the work of finding out what is happening somewhere, so that decisions can be made on fact rather than assumption. It is the single largest and most immediate application of autonomy in defence — and the one where the gap between what is needed and what is affordable is widest.

 The Problem

## Watching is expensive.

 § 01 / PROBLEM 

 Surveillance is fundamentally a problem of attention. Watching an area properly means watching it continuously, and human attention degrades badly over long, uneventful periods — which is precisely what good surveillance consists of. Staffing it properly is expensive; staffing it improperly is worse than not doing it.

 Reconnaissance has a different cost: to answer a question about a place, someone usually has to go there. That exposure is often the most dangerous part of an operation, and it is undertaken to obtain information rather than to achieve anything at the location itself.

 How Autonomy Changes It

## Persistent watch, without persistent staffing.

 An autonomous system does not get bored. It can hold a pattern for as long as its endurance allows, notice what changes, and escalate only what merits a person's attention.

 Persistence Sustained observation over long periods, at a cost that makes continuous coverage realistic.

 Reconnaissance without exposure Sending a machine to answer the question instead of a person.

 Conclusions, not raw feed Reporting what changed and why it might matter, rather than hours of video for someone to review.

 Attention where it counts Operators supervising several systems and spending their judgement on the exceptions.

 ISR Observe · Understand · Report 
 
 Persistence Limited by endurance, not attention 

 Reporting Structured findings, not raw video 

 Link Assumed intermittent 

 Decision Always made by a person 

 Stage Research & development 

 What It Demands

## Why ISR is a hard autonomy problem.

 § 02 / DEMANDS 

 01 
### Knowing what 'normal' is
 Flagging change requires a model of the baseline — which the system has to build for itself.
 02 
### Suppressing false alarms
 An ISR system that reports constantly is quickly ignored, which makes precision more valuable than sensitivity.
 03 
### Distance and scale
 The subjects of interest are usually far away and small in the frame.
 04 
### Endurance
 Persistence is an energy problem before it is a software problem.
 05 
### Bandwidth discipline
 There is rarely enough link to send everything, so the system must decide what is worth sending.
 06 
### Auditability
 Anything that informs a decision has to be reviewable afterwards.

 Everything described here is under active research and development . Nothing has been fielded, and we do not publish specifications or performance figures. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026 . Technical detail is shared directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms — get in touch .

 Application 02  ·  Force Protection

## Force protection.

 Force protection is the work of keeping people, vehicles and sites safe — largely by seeing a problem developing before it arrives. It is unglamorous, continuous, and consumes an enormous share of the people it is meant to protect.

 The Problem

## The guard force is drawn from the guarded.

 § 01 / PROBLEM 

 Protecting a site or a moving element means maintaining watch in every direction, continuously. The people doing that watching are drawn from the same limited group being protected, which means protection directly reduces the capacity available for everything else.

 It is also the classic vigilance task: long stretches of nothing punctuated by moments that matter enormously. Humans are poorly suited to that pattern and machines are well suited to it, which makes this one of the clearest cases for autonomy in the whole field.

 How Autonomy Helps

## Cover more ground with the same people.

 An autonomous system can maintain watch on an area indefinitely within its endurance, and only involve a person when something merits attention.

 Continuous watch Sustained observation of approaches and perimeters without rotating people through shifts.

 Early warning More time between detection and arrival, which is the entire value of the function.

 Wider coverage Extending effective awareness well beyond line of sight from the site itself.

 Escalation, not noise Routine activity handled quietly; only genuine exceptions raised to an operator.

 Force Protection Watch · Warn 
 
 Function Early warning and continuous watch 

 Applies to Sites, convoys, deployed elements 

 Benefit Returns people to their primary task 

 Decision Response always directed by a person 

 Stage Research & development 

 Design Constraints

## What it must get right.

 § 02 / CONSTRAINTS 

 01 
### Very low false alarms
 A system that raises the alarm without cause is disabled within a week.

 02 
### All conditions
 Threats do not wait for good weather or daylight.

 03 
### Low logistics burden
 It cannot demand more support than the watch it replaces.

 04 
### Predictable behaviour
 The team must know exactly what the system will and won't do.

 Everything described here is under active research and development . Nothing has been fielded, and we do not publish specifications or performance figures. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026 . Technical detail is shared directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms — get in touch .

 Application 03  ·  Counter-UAS

## Counter-UAS.

 Small uncrewed aircraft have become one of the defining problems in modern defence. They are cheap, numerous, difficult to see and easy to obtain — and the systems traditionally used to counter them cost orders of magnitude more than the thing they are countering.

 The Problem

## An economics problem as much as a technical one.

 § 01 / PROBLEM 

 A small drone can be inexpensive, while a conventional means of stopping it can cost a great deal. That exchange rate is unsustainable for anyone defending against numbers, and it is why counter-UAS has moved from a niche concern to a central one so quickly.

 The detection problem is genuinely hard on its own terms. Small aircraft are physically tiny, fly low and slow, are often made of materials that are difficult to detect, and appear against cluttered backgrounds. Distinguishing one from a bird at useful range is not a solved problem.

 Where Autonomy Applies

## Detect, track, identify.

 Our interest is the sensing and understanding half of the problem: reliably noticing that something is there, following it, and working out what it is — quickly enough for a person to decide what to do.

 Detection Noticing a small, low, slow object against a cluttered background, in all conditions.

 Tracking Holding onto it consistently as it manoeuvres, and handling several at once.

 Identification Distinguishing an aircraft from a bird, and one type of aircraft from another.

 Timely reporting Presenting a clear picture fast enough that the warning is still useful.

 Counter-UAS Detect · Track · Identify 
 
 Focus Sensing and understanding 

 Difficulty Small, low, slow, cluttered 

 Multiple targets Must handle more than one at a time 

 Response Decided and directed by a person 

 Stage Research & development 

 Our work in this area concerns detection, tracking and identification — building an accurate picture so that people can decide what to do. Decisions about response rest with the human commanders responsible for them, in line with our responsible autonomy commitments. Everything described here is under active research and development . Nothing has been fielded, and we do not publish specifications or performance figures. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026 . Technical detail is shared directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms — get in touch .

 Research & Concepts

## Ideas we're working on.

 A look at the research directions that shape where Rewind Dynamics is headed —
 the harder problems in autonomy we're exploring for defence and military applications. These are
 concepts and open questions, not finished products. We describe the idea; the engineering we keep for
 the people who need it.

 How To Read This Page

## Directions, not datasheets.

 Everything below is early-stage research. We
 share the shape of each idea and why it matters for defence — deliberately at a high level. No
 specifications, no performance figures, no operational detail. Serious discussion happens directly
 with partners, evaluators and the armed forces, under appropriate terms.

 § 00 / SCOPE 

 01 
### Concept-level
 We explain the intent and the value — not how it's built.

 02 
### Defence-focused
 Every direction is framed for defence and military use.

 03 
### Human-in-command
 A person sets the rules and stays responsible throughout.

 04 
### In R&D
 Nothing here is fielded. These are problems we're actively studying.

 Flagship Concept

## Two-tier autonomy: a mother, and its children.

 § 01 / NANO-DRONE 

 One of our most exciting research
 directions is a two-tier "mother–child" architecture for autonomous nano-drones. A
 larger carrier platform — the "mother" — travels to the area of interest and releases a group of very
 small, expendable "child" drones to do the close-in work.

 The idea is a division of labour. The mother carries range, endurance,
 compute and communications; the children carry almost nothing but their sensors and their autonomy.
 Because the children are tiny, they can go where a larger aircraft can't — low, close, and quiet —
 while the mother stays back, coordinates them and relays what they find.

 For defence, that opens up reconnaissance and
 observation in cluttered, confined or contested spaces without putting a person or an expensive
 platform forward. The children act as a forward layer of eyes; the mother is the brain and the link
 back to the people in command.

 Mother · Children Architecture 

 01 
### The mother
 Range, endurance and compute. It carries the children in, coordinates them, and holds the link back to the operator.
 
 02 
### The children
 Tiny, low-cost and expendable. They go close and low to sense what a large platform never could — and are meant to be lost without loss.
 
 03 
### Shared autonomy
 The two tiers think as one system — the mother planning, the children executing, each adapting as the picture changes.
 
 04 
### Why it matters
 Reach into confined, contested or dangerous spaces without putting people or costly aircraft forward.

 Concept

## Autonomous surveillance & ISR.

 A second direction is persistent, autonomous
 observation — intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance that runs with minimal operator load. The
 aim is simple to state: watch an area reliably, understand what's normal, and flag what isn't — so a
 human can decide what it means.

 We're deliberately keeping this one high-level. The value for defence is a
 forward set of patient, discreet eyes that reduce risk to personnel and extend how much a small team
 can keep watch over. A person always sets the tasking and stays in command of what's done with it.

 Observe · Understand · Alert ISR 
 
 Persistent Watch reliably, over long periods 

 Discreet Low signature, minimal footprint 

 Pattern-aware Learn what's normal, surface what isn't 

 Human-decided People judge meaning and response 

 More Directions

## Other problems we're exploring.

 The hard, shared problems underneath everything
 above. Progress on any of these lifts every platform we build.

 § 02 / OPEN QUESTIONS 

 01 

### Swarming
 Many small autonomous systems acting as one coordinated team — sharing what they see, splitting the task, and staying useful even if some are lost.
 
 02 

### GPS-denied navigation
 Knowing where you are and finding your way when satellite signals are jammed, spoofed or simply unavailable — using what the system can see and sense.
 
 03 

### Onboard perception
 Making sense of a cluttered, changing world in real time, on the platform itself — the difference between reacting and truly understanding.
 
 04 

### Edge intelligence
 Running capable autonomy on tiny, power-limited hardware, so a small system stays effective without a constant link home.
 
 05 

### Trustworthy autonomy
 Autonomy that stays predictable, safe and reviewable under stress — behaviour a commander can rely on and account for afterwards.
 
 06 

### Human–machine teaming
 The right hand-offs between operator and system, so autonomy amplifies a person's judgement instead of replacing it.

 Ground Rules

## How we research.

 Ideas are cheap; disciplined research is not.
 A few principles hold across everything on this page.

 § 03 / PRINCIPLES 

 01 
### Simulate first
 We prove ideas in software before they ever touch hardware.

 02 
### Rewind & assess
 Every run is recorded and reviewed honestly — the idea behind our name.

 03 
### Human in command
 People set the rules and stay responsible; machines carry out tasks.

 04 
### Restraint on detail
 We share the idea, not the sensitive specifics. Serious talk happens privately.

 Everything on this page describes
 research directions and concepts under active study at Rewind Dynamics. Nothing here is a product,
 specification, or claim of a fielded capability. All systems remain in research and development; our first
 real-world mission test is planned for December 2026.

 If you're a partner, evaluator or engineer who cares about these problems, we'd like to hear from you. Detail is shared privately, under appropriate terms.
