 Research  ·  Swarm Autonomy

## Swarm autonomy.

 A swarm is not simply a lot of drones. It is a group of autonomous systems that behave as one team — dividing a task between them, sharing what each of them sees, and continuing to work when individual members drop out. That last property is what makes the idea powerful.

 The Idea

## Resilience through numbers.

 § 01 / RATIONALE 

 A single capable platform is a single point of failure. Lose it and the mission stops. A group of cheaper, individually less capable platforms fails differently: losing one degrades the group slightly rather than ending the task, and the cost of that loss is proportionate.

 That changes what is reasonable to attempt. Tasks that would be unacceptable to risk an expensive aircraft on become straightforward when the platform involved is inexpensive and the group can absorb its loss. It also changes coverage — many sensors in many places see more than one sensor in one place.

 What Makes It A Swarm

## Coordination, not just quantity.

 The engineering question is how a group reaches sensible collective behaviour without a central controller telling every member what to do — because that controller becomes the single point of failure the swarm was meant to eliminate.

 Task division Splitting an objective between members and reallocating when circumstances change.

 Shared picture Combining what each member observes into an understanding none of them had alone.

 Decentralised decisions Local decisions that add up to sensible group behaviour without constant central direction.

 Graceful attrition Continuing to function, with proportionate loss of capability, as members drop out.

 Swarm Decentralised 
 
 Unit of value The group, not the individual 

 Failure mode Degrade, not stop 

 Communication Assumed limited and intermittent 

 Command One operator tasks the group 

 Stage Concept-level research 

 Open Questions

## What we're still working out.

 This is early research. We describe the shape of the problem rather than claiming it solved.

 § 02 / QUESTIONS 

 01 
### Tasking many as one
 How a single operator directs a group without workload growing with its size.
 02 
### Talking sparingly
 Coordination that survives very limited and unreliable communication between members.
 03 
### Avoiding each other
 Many platforms in a small volume without collisions or interference.
 04 
### Predictable group behaviour
 Emergent behaviour that a commander can actually anticipate.
 05 
### Cost per unit
 The economics only work if individual members are genuinely inexpensive.
 06 
### Accountability at scale
 Keeping human command meaningful when the group is large.

 Swarm autonomy is a concept-level research direction at Rewind Dynamics, described here at a high level by design. Everything described here is under active research and development . Nothing has been fielded, and we do not publish specifications or performance figures. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026 . Technical detail is shared directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms — get in touch .

 Explore Further

## Related reading.

 01 
### Research & concepts
 The mother–child nano-drone architecture and our other research directions.
 02 
### Tactical miniature systems
 The small, low-cost platforms swarming depends on.
 03 
### Responsible autonomy
 How human command works when there are many systems.

 Reference  ·  Glossary

## Defence autonomy, in plain English.

 Autonomy has accumulated a lot of jargon, and much of it obscures more than it
 explains. This is our working glossary — the terms we use across this site, defined the way we would
 explain them to someone in the room. No marketing, no acronym soup.

 The Vocabulary

## The terms that matter.

 Grouped by how they are actually used rather
 than alphabetically — starting with the ideas everything else depends on.

 § 01 / GLOSSARY 

### Autonomy
 The ability of a machine to carry out a task without a person directing each step. Autonomy is a spectrum, not a switch: a system may plan its own route while still asking a human before doing anything consequential.
 
### Autonomous system
 A platform that can sense its surroundings, decide what to do and act on that decision. At Rewind Dynamics this covers unmanned aerial, precision-guided and tactical platforms.
 
### UAV / UAS
 Unmanned aerial vehicle, or unmanned aerial system. UAV usually means the aircraft itself; UAS means the whole system — aircraft, ground control, communications and operators.
 
### ISR
 Intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. The work of gathering information about an area or situation so that commanders can make informed decisions.
 
### Surveillance
 Watching an area persistently over time to understand what is normal and notice what changes.
 
### Reconnaissance
 Going to look at a specific place to answer a specific question, usually once and quickly.
 
### Force protection
 Measures that keep personnel, equipment and sites safe — including early warning of an approaching threat.
 
### Sense–decide–act
 The core loop every autonomous system runs, many times a second: take in the world, choose an action, carry it out, and repeat. Making that loop fast, reliable and safe is the central engineering problem.
 
### Perception
 Turning raw camera and sensor data into a usable understanding of the environment — what is there, where it is, and whether it matters.
 
### Sensor fusion
 Combining several different sensors into a single picture that is more reliable than any one sensor could be alone.
 
### Edge AI
 Running artificial intelligence on the platform itself rather than in a remote data centre, so the system stays effective without a constant communications link.
 
### GPS-denied navigation
 Knowing your position and finding your way when satellite navigation is jammed, spoofed or simply unavailable — typically by using vision and onboard sensors instead.
 
### GNSS
 Global navigation satellite system: the general term for satellite positioning networks, of which GPS is one.
 
### SLAM
 Simultaneous localisation and mapping. Building a map of an unknown space while also working out where you are within it.
 
### Swarm
 A group of autonomous systems that coordinate as one team — sharing what they see, dividing the task, and remaining useful even if some are lost.
 
### Mother–child architecture
 A two-tier design in which a larger carrier platform transports and coordinates a group of much smaller platforms, which do the close-in work. One of our active research directions.
 
### Nano-drone
 A very small unmanned aircraft, typically light enough to be carried in quantity and cheap enough to be treated as expendable.
 
### SWaP
 Size, weight and power — the three constraints that dominate the design of any small autonomous system. Every capability added costs something in at least one of them.
 
### Man-portable
 Small and light enough to be carried and deployed by one person alongside their existing equipment.
 
### Dismounted
 Operating on foot, away from a vehicle. Dismounted teams have the tightest constraints on what they can carry.
 
### Tactical edge
 The forward, close-range environment where information is scarce, links are unreliable and decisions are made under pressure.
 
### Degraded link
 A communications connection that has become slow, intermittent or unusable. Well-designed autonomy continues behaving sensibly when this happens.
 
### Human-in-the-loop
 An arrangement where the system cannot take a significant action until a person approves it.
 
### Human-on-the-loop
 An arrangement where the system acts on its own but a person supervises continuously and can intervene or stop it at any time.
 
### Human in command
 Our own framing, and our operating principle: machines carry out tasks, but people set the rules, define the limits and remain responsible for the outcome.
 
### Autonomy stack
 The layered software architecture that produces autonomous behaviour — from low-level control, through perception and planning, up to mission and oversight.
 
### Guidance, navigation and control
 The three related jobs of deciding where to go, knowing where you are, and making the platform actually do it.
 
### Simulation-first
 Developing and proving behaviour in software before committing it to hardware, because software tests are faster, safer and repeatable.
 
### After-action assessment
 Reviewing a recorded run honestly to establish what went right, what went wrong and why — the discipline our name refers to.
 
### Payload
 Whatever a platform carries to do its job — usually sensors. Payload always competes with endurance for the same limited energy.
 
### Endurance
 How long a platform can operate before it must return, recharge or refuel.
 
### Teleoperation
 Direct remote control of a machine by a person. Distinct from autonomy, where the machine decides for itself within set limits.

 These are working definitions written for
 clarity, not formal doctrine — usage varies between organisations and countries. If you think one of them
 is wrong or could be clearer, tell us and we'll fix it.

 See It Applied

## From definitions to systems.

 These ideas are what we actually build with. See how they come together in our technology and the systems we're developing.

 Our Technology 
 Our Systems 

 Two terms deserve more than a definition: levels of autonomy and multi-sensor fusion each have their own page.

 Responsibility

## Autonomy you can trust.

 Autonomy for defence carries real responsibility. We treat safety, human command and accountability not as add-ons, but as design requirements — built in from the first line of code.

 Our Commitments

## Principles we design toward.

 These aren't slogans. Each one shapes how we
 architect, build and assess our systems.

 § 01 / PRINCIPLES 

 01 
### Human In Command
 A person is always in command. Machines carry out tasks; people decide whether they should happen, and remain responsible.

 02 
### Human Oversight
 Systems are designed so a person can supervise and intervene at any time — the leash is as long or short as the task requires.

 03 
### Safety By Design
 Clear operating limits and safe, predictable behaviour are built in from the start, not bolted on afterwards.

 04 
### Lawful & Ethical Use
 We build to be used lawfully and responsibly, within applicable rules and the direction of legitimate authorities.

 05 
### Accountability
 Decisions and runs are recorded so they can be understood and reviewed after the fact. Accountability by construction.

 06 
### Honest Assessment
 After every run we assess plainly — what went right, what went wrong, and why — and act on it.

 07 
### Security
 Sound security engineering as a default across the whole stack, from supply chain to runtime.

 08 
### Restraint
 We are deliberate about what we build and how we describe it. We would rather under-claim and over-deliver.

 The Core Idea

## People decide. Machines execute.

 Autonomy is useful precisely because a system can
 carry out a task without being steered moment to moment. But carrying out a task and deciding whether it
 should happen are two different things — and the second always belongs to people.

 Our systems are built to keep that line clear: bounded behaviour, a human able to
 supervise and stop them, and a full record afterwards. That is what makes autonomy something an
 institution can actually adopt with confidence.

 How we build it → 

 Guardrails By Design 
 
 Command A person is always in command 

 Bounds Clear limits on what a system will do 

 Intervene Supervise and stop at any time 

 Record Every decision logged and reviewable 

 Assess Honest after-action review, every run

 We're glad to discuss how we think about responsible autonomy.

 Company  ·  Ethics

## Ethics and business conduct.

 Defence is an industry where conduct matters more than usual, because the consequences of the work are real and the oversight is rightly strict. These are the standards we hold ourselves to — written plainly, so they can actually be held against us.

 Why Write This Down

## Culture is set early, or not at all.

 § 01 / PURPOSE 

 Codes of conduct have a reputation for being documents nobody reads, written to satisfy an auditor. We are writing this at a stage where the entire company can fit in one room, precisely because that is when the standard is actually set — by what gets tolerated, not by what gets published.

 Everything below applies to everyone at Rewind Dynamics without exception, and we expect the same from the partners and suppliers who work with us.

 Our Standards

## What we hold to.

 § 02 / STANDARDS 

 01 
### Honesty about capability
 We do not overstate what our systems can do. Nothing has been fielded, and we say so on every page that describes a system. Exaggeration in defence costs lives downstream, not just credibility.
 02 
### Integrity in competition
 We compete on the merit of the engineering. No bribes, no facilitation payments, no improper inducements, no arrangements that would embarrass us if published.
 03 
### Conflicts of interest
 Declared, not managed quietly. If a personal interest could reasonably look like it influenced a decision, it gets disclosed.
 04 
### Confidentiality
 Information shared with us under terms stays under those terms — from partners, programmes and competitors alike.
 05 
### Lawful conduct
 We work within export-control, sanctions, trade and employment law wherever we operate. See security & compliance .
 06 
### Respect at work
 Harassment, discrimination and bullying are grounds for removal. A small team offers nowhere for that to hide, and we intend to keep it that way.

 Speaking Up

## Raising a concern.

 A standard is only real if raising a breach is safe and straightforward. At our current size the route is deliberately simple and direct.

 Anyone can raise anything Concerns about conduct, safety, legality or a claim we have made publicly can be raised with any member of the leadership.

 In writing, if preferred Write to ethics@rewinddynamics.com . It is read directly, not routed through a system.

 No retaliation Raising a concern in good faith will not disadvantage anyone, regardless of whether the concern turns out to be correct.

 From outside too Partners, suppliers and members of the public can use the same address.

 Raising A Concern Direct 
 
 Internally Any member of leadership 

 In writing ethics@rewinddynamics.com 

 Security issues security@rewinddynamics.com 

 Retaliation Not tolerated, in any form 

 Applies to Employees, partners, suppliers 

 What We Expect Of Partners

## The same standard.

 § 03 / PARTNERS 

 01 
### Lawful operation
 Compliance with applicable export-control, sanctions and trade obligations.

 02 
### Honest representation
 Datasheets and claims that hold up under our testing, and a straight answer when they will not.

 03 
### No improper payments
 The same anti-bribery standard we hold ourselves to.

 04 
### Human command respected
 Our systems are built so a person stays in command. We will not adapt that for anyone.

 This page states our standards and our current practice; it is not a legal instrument and does not create contractual obligations. It will be expanded and formalised as the company grows. Last reviewed August 2026.

 Company  ·  Human Rights

## Human rights.

 Building autonomous systems for defence carries a direct responsibility to think about how they could be used, and by whom. This sets out our position, the checks we apply, and the limits we will not move.

 Why This Page Exists

## The technology makes it unavoidable.

 § 01 / CONTEXT 

 A company building autonomous systems cannot treat human rights as a procurement formality. The technology we develop can reduce risk to people — that is the point of it — but the same capability, misapplied or supplied to the wrong party, could do the opposite.

 We would rather state our limits publicly, before commercial pressure makes them inconvenient, than discover them under it.

 Our Commitments

## Lines we hold.

 § 02 / COMMITMENTS 

 01 
### A person is always in command
 Machines carry out tasks; people set the rules and remain accountable. We will not build a system designed to remove a human from that role, and this is not negotiable commercially.
 02 
### End-use and end-user assessment
 Before we engage, we assess what a system would be used for and by whom, alongside sanctions and export-control screening. Any one of these can stop the engagement.
 03 
### We decline work
 Where we judge that a party is unable or unwilling to use a system lawfully and responsibly, we decline — and we accept the commercial cost of that.
 04 
### Compliance with applicable law
 We operate within international humanitarian law obligations as they apply through the jurisdictions and customers we work with.
 05 
### Accountability by design
 Our systems record what they did and why, so decisions can be reconstructed and someone can be answerable for them.
 06 
### Labour standards
 We expect fair, lawful and safe employment throughout our own operations and our supply chain.

 Supply Chain

## What we expect of suppliers.

 Our supply chain is currently small, which makes it practical to know who we buy from and to ask directly rather than rely on attestations alone.

 No forced or child labour We do not knowingly work with suppliers using forced, bonded, trafficked or child labour, at any tier we can see.

 Lawful employment Fair wages, lawful hours and safe conditions for the people who make what we buy.

 Willingness to answer Suppliers should expect to be asked, and to be able to answer. Reluctance to answer is itself information.

 Cascade of expectation We expect suppliers to hold their own suppliers to a comparable standard.

 Supply Chain Expectations 
 
 Scale Small and directly known 

 Screening Sanctions and export-control 

 Labour Forced and child labour prohibited 

 Escalation ethics@rewinddynamics.com 

 Last reviewed August 2026 

 If you believe a Rewind Dynamics system, supplier or engagement raises a human rights concern, write to ethics@rewinddynamics.com . Concerns raised in good faith are taken seriously and will not be met with retaliation. This statement describes our position and current practice; it will be formalised and expanded as the company grows.

 Company  ·  Governance

## Governance and oversight.

 Governance in a company our size is not a committee structure — it is a small number of decisions that require more than one person to agree, and a record of why each was made. This describes how that actually works today.

 The Principle

## Some decisions must not rest with one person.

 § 01 / PRINCIPLE 

 Most decisions in an early-stage company should be fast and individual. A small number should not be, because getting them wrong is not recoverable: what we agree to build, who we agree to supply, what we claim publicly, and how much autonomy a system is permitted.

 Our governance is deliberately narrow and concrete. Rather than describing an aspirational board structure, we name the specific decisions that require review and who has to be involved.

 Reserved Decisions

## Decisions that require more than one person.

 These cannot be taken unilaterally, regardless of who is asking or how commercially attractive the request is.

 § 02 / RESERVED 

 01 
### What we agree to build
 Any new programme or significant capability change is reviewed against our responsible autonomy commitments before work starts.
 02 
### Who we agree to supply
 End-use and end-user assessment, sanctions and export-control screening, and a judgement about lawful use. Any one of these can stop an engagement.
 03 
### Degree of autonomy permitted
 Where a system sits on the spectrum between operator-directed and self-directed is a governance decision, not an engineering preference.
 04 
### Public claims
 What we say a system can do is reviewed before publication. Our systems are in R&D and every page must say so.
 05 
### Safety-relevant changes
 Changes affecting safety limits, failure behaviour or the operator's ability to intervene require review and a recorded rationale.
 06 
### Handling of sensitive material
 Whether and how we accept classified, export-controlled or proprietary information from a third party.

 How It Works Today

## Small, but not informal.

 At our size, governance runs through a handful of practices rather than a hierarchy. Each is designed to survive the company getting larger.

 Recorded rationale Reserved decisions are written down with the reasoning, not just the outcome. A decision nobody can reconstruct cannot be reviewed.

 Separation of advocate and approver Whoever wants to do the thing is not the only person who approves it.

 Escalation is expected Raising a decision upward is treated as good judgement, never as an inability to decide.

 Reviewed as we grow These practices are reviewed periodically and will formalise into a board and defined committees as scale requires.

 Governance Current Practice 
 
 Stage Early-stage private company 

 Reserved decisions Require more than one approver 

 Record Rationale written, not only outcome 

 Ethics route ethics@rewinddynamics.com 

 Last reviewed August 2026 

 We are a private, early-stage company. This page describes governance as it is actually practised today rather than a structure we intend to adopt later; it will be updated as the company formalises. We do not publish individual officer details at this stage.

 Company  ·  Security & Compliance

## Security and compliance.

 Working in defence carries obligations that go well beyond good engineering practice. How we handle information, who we work with, and what we are permitted to share are governed by law and by our own standards — and we take both seriously from the outset rather than retrofitting them later.

 Our Position

## Built in from the start.

 § 01 / POSITION 

 It is common for early-stage companies to treat security and compliance as something to formalise once they are larger. In defence that is the wrong order. The obligations attach to the work itself, not to the size of the company doing it, and habits formed early are the ones that persist.

 We are an R&D-stage company and we are candid about what that means: our programme is proportionate to our size and maturing as we grow. What follows describes how we operate today and the direction we are building toward, not a claim to certifications we do not yet hold.

 Information Security

## Protecting what we hold.

 Most of what matters in an autonomy company is information: source code, models, test data, and whatever partners entrust to us. Protecting it is a first-order concern.

 Least privilege Access to systems and data is granted on need, reviewed, and removed when no longer required.

 Segregation Partner and programme material is kept separate, and handled according to whatever terms it arrived under.

 Secure development Security considered as part of engineering — dependencies, secrets handling, code review and change control.

 Incident readiness A defined route for identifying, containing and reporting a security incident.

 Information Security Practice 
 
 Principle Least privilege, by default 

 Partner material Segregated and handled per terms 

 Development Security reviewed as part of engineering 

 Disclosure security@rewinddynamics.com 

 Maturity Proportionate and growing 

 Regulatory

## Obligations we work within.

 Defence technology is regulated, and rightly so. These are the areas that govern what we can build, share and export.

 § 02 / REGULATORY 

 01 
### Export control & defence trade
 Autonomy and unmanned systems technology is subject to export-control regimes. We assess what may be shared, with whom, and under what authorisation before sharing it.
 02 
### Sanctions & screening
 We screen counterparties and will not work with entities subject to applicable restrictions.
 03 
### End-use and end-user
 We care who ultimately uses what we build, and we ask. Our responsible autonomy commitments are part of that assessment.
 04 
### Data protection
 Personal information submitted through this site is handled as set out in our privacy notice .
 05 
### Contractual confidentiality
 Programme and partner information is handled strictly under the terms it was shared with us.
 06 
### Anti-bribery & conduct
 We compete on the merits of the engineering. Nothing else is acceptable.

 Working With Us

## What this means in practice.

 § 03 / PRACTICE 

 01 
### Nothing sensitive by web form
 Please do not send classified, export-controlled or otherwise sensitive material through this website or unsecured email.

 02 
### We arrange the channel
 Tell us you have something to discuss and we will set up an appropriate route for it.

 03 
### We say no when required
 If a request falls outside what we may lawfully or responsibly do, we will say so plainly.

 04 
### Human command is a red line
 Our systems are built so a person remains in command. That is not a term we negotiate.

 Responsible disclosure. If you believe you have found a security vulnerability affecting Rewind Dynamics, please contact security@rewinddynamics.com with enough detail to reproduce it. Please give us a reasonable opportunity to investigate and remediate before disclosing publicly. We will acknowledge reports and keep you informed. This page describes our approach and is not a warranty or a statement of certification.

 Explore Further

## Related reading.

 01 
### Responsible autonomy
 Human command, safety limits, lawful use and accountability.
 02 
### Partners
 How we engage, and what we expect from those we work with.
 03 
### Quality & assurance
 How we establish that a system does what we say it does.

 Questions

## Need to discuss compliance?

 Company  ·  Quality & Assurance

## Quality and assurance.

 In defence, quality is not a finish; it is evidence. The question is never whether a system worked once, but whether you can demonstrate it will work again, explain why, and show the record. That standard shapes how we build.

 The Standard

## Evidence, not assertion.

 § 01 / STANDARD 

 Autonomy makes quality harder than conventional engineering. A traditional mechanism can be specified, tested against that specification and signed off. An autonomous system behaves differently in different circumstances by design, which means quality has to be established across a range of situations rather than at a single operating point.

 Our answer is to treat evidence as the deliverable. Every claim we make internally is expected to be backed by a recorded, repeatable result — and where we cannot yet demonstrate something, we say so rather than implying it.

 How We Assure

## The disciplines behind the claim.

 These practices are proportionate to our stage today and are being formalised as the company grows toward fielded systems.

 Traceable requirements Knowing why each requirement exists, and being able to point to the evidence that it is met.

 Repeatable verification Tests that can be re-run on demand and produce the same answer — the basis of every claim.

 Configuration control Knowing exactly what software and hardware are in any given unit, and being able to rebuild it exactly.

 Recorded runs Every simulated and physical run captured so it can be replayed, reviewed and audited later.

 Assurance Evidence-Led 
 
 Basis Recorded, repeatable results 

 Traceability Requirement to evidence 

 Configuration Reproducible builds 

 Review Honest after-action assessment 

 Maturity Proportionate and formalising 

 Our Commitments

## What we promise.

 § 02 / COMMITMENTS 

 01 
### We do not overstate
 If something has not been demonstrated, we will not imply that it has.

 02 
### We publish stage, not spin
 Our systems are in R&D and we say so on every page that describes them.

 03 
### We record failures
 A run that went wrong is more valuable than one that went right, and it is kept.

 04 
### We invite scrutiny
 Evaluators are welcome to examine our approach under appropriate terms.

 Everything described here is under active research and development . Nothing has been fielded, and we do not publish specifications or performance figures. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026 . Technical detail is shared directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms — get in touch .

 Company  ·  Responsibility

## Corporate responsibility.

 We are a small research-and-development company, and we intend to report on our responsibilities in proportion to that — honestly, without the language of a large corporation describing programmes it has not built yet.

 Our Stance

## Proportionate, and honest about it.

 § 01 / STANCE 

 Sustainability reporting in defence often runs ahead of substance. Companies our size are tempted to describe frameworks, targets and committees that exist largely on the page. We would rather state plainly what we actually do today, and expand this page as the company grows into more.

 That does not mean the topic is unimportant. The decisions a company makes early — how it treats people, what work it accepts, how it accounts for its footprint — are the ones that harden into culture. We are making those decisions now, deliberately.

 Where We Focus

## Four commitments we can stand behind.

 Each is something we practise today rather than an aspiration for a future scale we have not reached.

 § 02 / COMMITMENTS 

 01 
### Responsible engineering
 The most consequential environmental and ethical choices we make are in what we build and for whom. Our responsible autonomy commitments are the substantive part of this page, not an adjacent one.
 02 
### Our footprint
 We are a software-first company with a single engineering facility. Our direct footprint is modest — compute, a building, travel — and we prefer simulation to field testing partly because it consumes far less of all three.
 03 
### The people we employ
 Fair pay, honest hiring, and work that develops people technically. A small team means every hire matters, and so does how they are treated.
 04 
### What we decline
 Refusing work is a sustainability decision too. We do not build systems that remove a human from command, and we will not supply parties we judge unable to use them lawfully.

 Reporting

## What we will and won't claim.

 We would rather publish a short, true page than a long, impressive one. As the company grows, this section will grow with it — and we will date the changes.

 No certifications we don't hold We will not imply accreditation, audit or framework alignment we have not actually completed.

 No targets without a method A number without a way to measure it is marketing, not a commitment.

 Report the footprint honestly When we are large enough for measurement to be meaningful, we will measure and publish it.

 Expand as we grow This page will lengthen as the company does. Its current brevity is the accurate representation.

 Status Early Stage 
 
 Company size Small, growing engineering team 

 Facilities One engineering facility, New Delhi 

 Primary method Simulation-first development 

 Frameworks None claimed at this stage 

 Last reviewed August 2026 

 This page describes our approach and current practice. It is not an assurance statement and does not claim alignment with any reporting framework. Questions are welcome at info@rewinddynamics.com .

 Company  ·  Timeline

## 2020 to 2026.

 A short, honest record of how Rewind Dynamics has developed — the decisions that shaped the company, the programmes we opened, and the milestone still ahead of us. We have deliberately built foundations before announcing products.

 How To Read It

## Foundations first.

 § 01 / CONTEXT 

 Six years is a long time to work without a fielded product, and we are frequently asked about it. The answer is that autonomy rewards patience: the architecture decisions made early — running intelligence on the platform, keeping a human in command, proving behaviour in simulation before hardware — are extremely expensive to reverse later.

 So the timeline below is mostly a record of foundations: a position taken, a team assembled, a programme opened, an architecture settled. The milestone that matters most is the one still ahead — our first real-world mission test, planned for December 2026.

 Milestones

## The record so far.

 § 02 / MILESTONES 

 26 Jan 2020 
 
### Founded in New Delhi
 Rewind Dynamics is established with a single objective: build autonomous systems that defence and military users can genuinely trust.
 
 Aug 2020 
 
### A position on trustworthy autonomy
 We publish our view that the forces depending on autonomous systems should be able to inspect, adapt and own them.
 
 Mar 2021 
 
### Building the founding team
 Recruitment begins in earnest across autonomy, perception, robotics and embedded systems.
 
 Sep 2021 
 
### Committing to the edge
 We settle a foundational architectural decision: intelligence runs on the platform, never dependent on a link.
 
 May 2022 
 
### First unmanned aerial system programme
 Focused development begins on our first autonomous UAV.
 
 Nov 2022 
 
### Human always in command
 We formalise the principle that governs every system we build: machines execute, people decide.
 
 Feb 2024 
 
### Engineering facility expanded
 More space, better test infrastructure and room to grow the team in New Delhi.
 
 Apr 2025 
 
### Precision guidance programme opens
 A dedicated programme begins on navigation, perception and decision software for precision guidance.
 
 Jun 2026 
 
### The tactical edge thesis
 We set out why small autonomous systems change what a dismounted team can see and do.
 
 Dec 2026 
 
### First real-world mission test
 Planned: our first end-to-end mission test, moving from simulation into the physical world.

 Dates reflect company milestones and published positions. Our systems remain in active research and development ; nothing has been fielded. The December 2026 mission test is planned , not completed.

 Company  ·  Locations

## Where we work.

 One engineering facility, and customers wherever autonomy is needed. We are deliberately concentrated at this stage — the work benefits from everyone being in the same building — while the systems we build are intended for defence and military users worldwide.

 Our Footprint

## Concentrated by choice.

 § 01 / FOOTPRINT 

 Rewind Dynamics is headquartered in New Delhi, India, where our engineering facility, laboratory and test infrastructure sit together. At our stage that concentration is an advantage rather than a limitation: autonomy is developed by tight iteration between software, hardware and test, and that goes faster when the people doing it share a room.

 Being headquartered in one country says nothing about who we build for. Our systems are designed for defence and military users internationally, and we engage with programmes, primes and evaluators wherever they are — subject to the export-control and end-user assessment set out in our security & compliance and human rights pages.

 Headquarters

## New Delhi, India.

 Our headquarters and sole engineering facility. It houses software and hardware engineering, our simulation environment and our test infrastructure.

 Engineering Autonomy, perception, robotics and embedded systems, working alongside each other.

 Simulation The environment where most of our development and testing happens before hardware.

 Laboratory & test Bench and integration facilities, expanded in 2024 as the team grew.

 Correspondence General enquiries reach us at info@rewinddynamics.com; we arrange secure channels where needed.

 Headquarters New Delhi

 Partners & Programmes

## Who we work with.

 Serious autonomy is not built alone. We work with defence programmes, evaluators,
 integrators, suppliers and research institutions — and we are deliberately open about how to start a
 conversation with us, wherever in the world you are.

 Our Position

## We build the core. We integrate with the rest.

 § 01 / APPROACH 

 Rewind Dynamics is focused on the autonomy core — the software and
 engineering that let a platform sense, decide and act. We deliberately design that core to be modular,
 so it can sit alongside existing platforms, sensors and command arrangements rather than replacing them.

 That makes us a natural partner rather than a competitor to most of the
 defence supply chain. If you build airframes, sensors, radios or ground systems, our work is meant to
 make yours more capable — not to lock anyone into a closed stack.

 Partnership Types

## Four ways we engage.

 § 02 / ENGAGEMENT 

 01 
### Defence programmes & evaluators
 Armed forces, procurement bodies and evaluation teams assessing autonomous capability. We share technical detail privately, under appropriate terms, and welcome structured evaluation.
 Evaluation Programmes 
 
 02 
### Primes & integrators
 Platform builders and system integrators who need an autonomy layer that fits into an existing architecture instead of dictating it.
 Integration Platforms 
 
 03 
### Suppliers & component partners
 Sensors, compute, propulsion, communications and materials. If you make something we should be designing around, we'd like to know.
 Supply Hardware 
 
 04 
### Research institutions
 Universities and labs working on perception, control, swarming or GPS-denied navigation. Hard problems benefit from more than one group attacking them.
 Research Collaboration 

 How We Work

## Straightforward to deal with.

 We are an R&D-stage company and we behave
 like one. That means being precise about what exists today, and what is still being built.

 We don't over-claim Nothing has been fielded yet. We will tell you exactly what stage a capability is at.

 Detail goes private We publish the shape of our work, not specifications. Substance is shared directly, under appropriate terms.

 Lawful and compliant We work within applicable export-control and defence-trade rules, and we expect our partners to do the same.

 Human command, always Our systems are designed so a person sets the rules and stays responsible. That is not negotiable.

 Company  ·  Suppliers

## Suppliers and supply chain.

 We build the autonomy; we do not pretend to build everything else. Sensors, compute, propulsion, radios, structures and manufacturing all come from companies that do those things better than we could — and choosing them well is a genuine engineering decision, not a procurement formality.

 Our Approach

## Suppliers are design partners.

 § 01 / APPROACH 

 In a size-, weight- and power-constrained system, component choices dictate what is architecturally possible. A sensor's characteristics change what perception can achieve; a compute module's thermal envelope changes what autonomy can run. We would rather involve suppliers early, as design partners, than issue a specification at the end.

 We are a small company at an early stage, so we are direct about scale: our volumes today are development volumes. What we can offer instead is a serious technical relationship, clear requirements, and prompt, honest communication.

 What We Source

## Areas where we work with suppliers.

 If your company works in any of these areas, we would be glad to hear from you.

 § 02 / CATEGORIES 

 01 
### Sensors & imaging
 Cameras and sensing across conditions where ordinary imaging struggles — low light, poor weather, long range.
 02 
### Embedded compute
 Small, efficient compute capable of running real-time perception and autonomy within tight thermal and power limits.
 03 
### Propulsion & power
 Motors, drives, batteries and power management where efficiency directly buys endurance.
 04 
### Communications
 Radios and datalinks that behave sensibly when contested, congested or intermittent.
 05 
### Structures & materials
 Lightweight, rugged structures and the materials and processes behind them.
 06 
### Manufacturing & test
 Precision manufacture, assembly, and environmental or reliability test services.

 What We Look For

## How we choose.

 Beyond the obvious question of whether a component performs, these are the things that decide whether a supplier relationship works.

 Technical honesty Datasheets that hold up in our conditions, and a straight answer when something will not do what we need.

 Supply resilience Availability we can plan a programme around, and early warning of changes or obsolescence.

 Compliance Willingness and ability to work within applicable export-control and trade obligations.

 Engineering access Someone technical we can actually talk to when an integration question arises.

 Supplier Fit Criteria 
 
 Stage Development volumes today 

 Relationship Technical, early, direct 

 Compliance Export control and screening apply 

 Contact partnerships@rewinddynamics.com 

 Based New Delhi · sourcing worldwide 

 To introduce your company, email partnerships@rewinddynamics.com with a short description of what you make and where you think it fits. Please do not send sensitive, proprietary or export-controlled material in a first email — tell us it exists and we will arrange an appropriate channel. All engagements are subject to screening and applicable export-control obligations; see security & compliance .

 Rewind Dynamics is actively raising investment to accelerate its
 defence-autonomy programmes. We're building the autonomy behind unmanned aerial, precision-guided and tactical
 systems — and we're looking for partners who want to back that from the ground floor.

 Register Interest 
 
 investors@rewinddynamics.com 

 The Opportunity

## Autonomy is the defining defence technology of the decade.

 § 01 / OPPORTUNITY 

 Around the world, defence is moving decisively toward autonomous and
 uncrewed systems. Every serious force is investing in the ability to sense, decide and act without a
 human in every loop — and demand is set to grow for years to come.

 Yet trustworthy, software-first autonomy remains under-served. That is
 the gap Rewind Dynamics is built to fill: a focused team building the autonomy core that unmanned aerial,
 precision-guided and tactical platforms all depend on. Back the core, and you back every platform that runs on it.

 Tailwind 

## Structural demand
 Defence spending on autonomy and uncrewed systems is a durable, worldwide, multi-year tailwind.

 Timing 

## Early, foundational
 We're at the ground floor — building the core before the platforms scale around it.

 Inflection 

## First mission test
 Our first real-world mission test is planned for December 2026 — a meaningful milestone to back ahead of.

 proven-in-the-field.

 Engineering talent Growing the team across autonomy, perception, robotics and embedded systems.

 Prototyping & test Hardware, integration and the trials that take our systems into the real world.

 Facilities & compute The lab space and computing our R&D depends on.

 Frequently Asked

## Questions, answered.

 Straight answers about who we are, what we're building, where we are in the journey, and how to work with us.

 What does Rewind Dynamics do? Rewind Dynamics is a defence-technology company, based in New Delhi, that designs and develops autonomous systems — unmanned aerial (UAV), precision-guided and tactical platforms — for defence and military applications.

 When was the company founded? Rewind Dynamics was founded on 26 January 2020 in New Delhi, India.

 What stage are you at? Have your systems been tested or fielded? We are a research-and-development company. Our systems are under active development and have not been fielded or tested in the real world yet. Our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026.

 What systems are you building? Three families that share a common autonomy core: unmanned aerial systems (UAVs) for surveillance and force protection; precision guidance for accurate, accountable effects; and tactical miniature systems for close-range, dismounted use.

 Do you only work with India, or globally? We're headquartered in New Delhi, but we're a global company: we build autonomous systems for defence and military users worldwide. Our focus is autonomy you can trust, adapt and maintain on your own terms — capability that's owned end to end rather than treated as a sealed black box.

 How do you think about safety and ethics? A person is always in command. Machines carry out tasks; people set the rules and stay responsible. We design for human oversight, safety limits, lawful use, accountability and honest after-action assessment. See our Responsible Autonomy page.

 Do you publish specifications or performance figures? No. At this stage we don't publish specifications or performance figures. We share detail directly with partners, evaluators and the armed forces under appropriate terms.

 Can we partner with, or evaluate, your systems? Yes — we welcome conversations with partners, suppliers, programmes and evaluators. Please contact us and we'll take it from there.

 Are you raising investment? Yes, we are actively raising to accelerate our R&D. See our Investors page or write to investors@rewinddynamics.com.

 Are you hiring? Yes. We're building the founding engineering team across autonomy, perception, robotics and embedded systems. See our Careers page or write to careers@rewinddynamics.com.

 Where are you based, and how do we reach you? We're headquartered in New Delhi, India. For general enquiries, email info@rewinddynamics.com or use the contact form.

The Attention Problem in ISR | Rewind Dynamics 

 Skip to content 

 01 Home 
 02 Company 
 03 Systems 
 04 Capabilities 
 05 Applications 
 06 Technology 
 07 Research 
 08 Investors 
 09 Careers 
 10 Newsroom 
 11 Contact 

 Perspective 24 June 2025 New Delhi 

## The attention problem

 Cameras are cheap and can go almost anywhere. What is scarce is the attention needed to look at what they produce — and that, not sensing, is the real constraint on surveillance.

 Surveillance rarely fails for lack of sensors. Cameras are inexpensive and can be placed almost anywhere. What is scarce is not imagery — it is the attention required to look at it.

## The vigilance problem

 Watching is a task humans perform poorly over long periods, and the research on this is not ambiguous. Sustained attention on a low-event task degrades measurably within tens of minutes. The irony is exact: good surveillance consists overwhelmingly of uneventful time, which is precisely the condition under which human vigilance is least reliable.

 So an organisation faces an unattractive choice. Staff surveillance properly — rotating people frequently enough to maintain attention, which is expensive and consumes the same personnel needed elsewhere. Or staff it improperly, and hold coverage that exists on paper but not in practice.

 Adding cameras without adding attention does not increase surveillance. It increases unreviewed footage. 

## What autonomy actually changes

 An autonomous system does not become bored. It can hold a pattern for as long as endurance allows, and — more importantly — it can decide what deserves a person's attention rather than requiring a person to find it.

 That inverts the workflow. Instead of a human watching a feed hoping to notice something, the system watches continuously and escalates exceptions. The human's attention is spent on judgement, which is what humans are actually good at, rather than on detection, which they are not.

## The baseline problem

 Reporting what changed requires knowing what normal looks like — and normal is specific to a place and a time of day, not something that can be shipped in advance. The system has to build that understanding itself, from observation, and keep updating it as conditions and seasons shift.

 This is genuinely hard, and it is where a lot of otherwise capable systems disappoint. A model that flags everything unusual will flag weather, wildlife, shadows and ordinary activity. A model tuned until it stops doing that often stops flagging what matters too.

## False alarms are the whole game

 We would argue that precision matters more than sensitivity in this application, which is not the conventional emphasis. The reasoning is behavioural rather than technical: a system that raises the alarm without cause trains its operators to ignore it, and an ignored system provides no coverage regardless of how good its detection is on paper.

 So the metric we care about is not how much a system detects, but how much of what it reports is worth reporting — and whether the confidence it attaches to a report is honest enough to act on.

## Bandwidth as a forcing function

 There is rarely enough communications capacity to send everything, which turns out to be a useful constraint rather than only a limitation. It forces the system to decide what is worth transmitting, which is the same discipline that makes its reports useful to a person.

 Sending conclusions rather than raw video is better on every axis: less bandwidth, less exposure, and far less human time consumed at the other end. It also requires the system to be right about what matters, which is the harder engineering but the correct target.

## Why this shapes what we build

 ISR is the largest and most immediate application of autonomy in defence, and the attention economics are why. It is also why our work concentrates on perception quality and honest uncertainty rather than on platform performance figures — the limiting factor was never how long something can stay airborne.

 — Rewind Dynamics · Perspective

The Autonomy Decade — Software as Capability | Rewind Dynamics 

 Skip to content 

 01 Home 
 02 Company 
 03 Systems 
 04 Capabilities 
 05 Applications 
 06 Technology 
 07 Research 
 08 Investors 
 09 Careers 
 10 Newsroom 
 11 Contact 

 Perspective 14 July 2026 New Delhi 

## The autonomy decade

 Defence advantage used to be measured in things you could point at. Increasingly it is measured in what a system can do on its own — and that changes how capability should be built, bought and maintained.

 For most of the last century, defence capability was measured in things you could point at. Range, payload, armour, speed. Procurement cycles were organised around delivering objects, and an advantage, once built, tended to last for years because the object itself was hard to reproduce.

 That logic is breaking down. Increasingly, the decisive difference between two similar platforms is not the platform — it is what the platform can do on its own. And that lives in software.

## The advantage moved

 Consider two aircraft with identical airframes, sensors and engines. One requires a trained operator giving continuous input. The other can be given an objective and left to pursue it, reporting back only what matters. These are not two versions of the same capability. They are different capabilities entirely, and the difference is entirely software.

 This has an uncomfortable implication for how defence organisations buy things. A software advantage does not behave like a hardware advantage. It can be improved continuously rather than at refit intervals. It can be copied and deployed across a fleet at negligible marginal cost. And it decays quickly if it is not maintained, because the state of the art moves underneath it.

 An advantage you cannot modify is an advantage with an expiry date attached. 

## Why sealed systems are a trap

 If the decisive component is software, then the ability to inspect, understand and change that software is not a procurement nicety. It is the capability itself. A force that operates autonomous systems it cannot examine has outsourced the most consequential part of its own decision-making to a supplier.

 This is the reasoning behind our position that defence users should be able to own the autonomy they depend on. Not necessarily to write it themselves, but to understand it, adapt it, and improve it on their own terms and timeline rather than someone else's.

## What this means for how systems are built

 If software is where the advantage lives, the engineering priorities change. Three consequences follow, and they have shaped how we build:

 The core matters more than the platform. An autonomy core that works across unmanned aerial, precision-guided and tactical systems compounds: an improvement made for one benefits all three. Building three bespoke stacks does not.

 Iteration speed is a capability. How quickly you can test, learn and improve determines where you end up. That is why we develop simulation-first — a scenario that takes a day in the field can run thousands of times overnight in software.

 Modularity is strategic, not aesthetic. Clean interfaces mean the autonomy can integrate with existing platforms and command arrangements rather than demanding everything be replaced around it.

## The uncomfortable part

 There is a version of this argument that becomes triumphalism about software eating defence. We would resist that. Hardware still decides what is physically possible; an autonomy stack cannot give an aircraft endurance it does not have. Systems engineering, ruggedness and manufacturing remain genuinely hard, and are where most promising prototypes actually die.

 The honest claim is narrower: the marginal advantage has moved. Between two competent platforms, the one that thinks better wins — and thinking is improvable in a way that airframes are not.

## Where we sit

 Rewind Dynamics was founded in 2020 on this thesis, and we have spent the years since building the core rather than rushing a product to market. Our systems remain in research and development; our first end-to-end mission test is planned for December 2026. We would rather state that plainly than imply more.

 If the thesis is right, the next decade of defence capability will be decided by organisations that treat autonomy as something to own and improve continuously — not as a feature to purchase once. That is the bet we are making.

 — Rewind Dynamics · Perspective 
 Back to Insights

The Cost Curve Problem — Counter-UAS | Rewind Dynamics 

 Skip to content 

 01 Home 
 02 Company 
 03 Systems 
 04 Capabilities 
 05 Applications 
 06 Technology 
 07 Research 
 08 Investors 
 09 Careers 
 10 Newsroom 
 11 Contact 

 Perspective 9 September 2025 New Delhi 

## The cost curve problem

 Counter-UAS is usually discussed as a sensing problem. It is more usefully understood as arithmetic — and the arithmetic is what makes it urgent.

 Counter-UAS is usually discussed as a sensing and effects problem. It is more usefully understood as an arithmetic problem, because the arithmetic is what makes it urgent.

## The exchange rate

 If a threat can be produced for a small sum and the established method of stopping it costs orders of magnitude more, the defender loses the exchange even while winning every engagement. Sustained against numbers, that is not a tactical inconvenience — it is a resourcing failure.

 What makes small uncrewed aircraft genuinely awkward is that they sit precisely in the gap between existing categories. They are too small and slow for systems designed against fast aircraft, too numerous for engagement methods that assume a handful of targets, and too cheap for the exchange rate to work in the defender's favour.

 You can win every engagement and still lose, if each win costs more than the thing you destroyed. 

## Detection is harder than it sounds

 Before anything else, you have to see it — and small aircraft are legitimately difficult to detect. They are physically tiny, fly low and slowly, are frequently made of materials that return little to conventional sensing, and appear against cluttered backgrounds of terrain, buildings and vegetation.

 Then there is the discrimination problem. At useful range, distinguishing a small aircraft from a bird is not trivial, and getting it wrong in either direction is costly: miss the aircraft and the system has failed; flag every bird and the system is switched off within a week.

 Small physical size at operationally useful ranges.

 Low and slow flight profiles that many sensing approaches were not designed for.

 Cluttered backgrounds rather than open sky.

 Multiple simultaneous tracks rather than one.

 The need to identify, not merely detect.

## Where autonomy actually helps

 Our interest is deliberately confined to the sensing and understanding half: reliably noticing something is there, holding a track on it as it manoeuvres, handling several at once, and working out what it is — fast enough that the warning still has value.

 This is a perception problem of the hardest kind, which is why it connects directly to the rest of our work. Small, distant objects in clutter, in poor conditions, with a very low tolerance for false alarms, running on constrained compute. Improvements here benefit every other application we build for.

## Where we stop

 What happens after identification — whether and how to respond — is a decision for the human commanders responsible for it. We build the picture; people decide what to do about it. That boundary follows directly from our position that a person is always in command , and we are explicit about it because in this application the distinction matters more than most.

## The honest position

 Counter-UAS is not solved, by us or by anyone. It is a genuinely hard sensing problem attached to a genuinely hard economic one, and the threat side is improving quickly and cheaply. Our systems remain in research and development.

 What we can say is that the shape of a workable answer is fairly clear: detection that holds up in real conditions, discrimination good enough to be trusted, and a cost structure that does not lose the exchange. Getting all three at once is the work.

 — Rewind Dynamics · Perspective 
 Back to Insights

The Case for Thinking at the Edge | Rewind Dynamics 

 Skip to content 

 01 Home 
 02 Company 
 03 Systems 
 04 Capabilities 
 05 Applications 
 06 Technology 
 07 Research 
 08 Investors 
 09 Careers 
 10 Newsroom 
 11 Contact 

 Perspective 27 January 2026 New Delhi 

## The case for thinking at the edge

 Cloud inference assumes a fast, reliable, permanently available link. In defence that assumption fails routinely — so the intelligence has to live on the platform, and that constrains everything.

 A great deal of modern artificial intelligence assumes a data centre. Models are large, compute is abundant, and the network connecting the two is fast and permanently available. Almost none of those assumptions hold on a platform operating in contested space.

 This is not a preference or an optimisation. For defence autonomy, running intelligence on the platform is a structural requirement, and it constrains every engineering decision downstream.

## Four reasons, in order of severity

 Availability. Links are jammed, saturated, blocked by terrain, or simply out of range. A system that stops thinking when the radio drops is a system nobody can plan a mission around.

 Latency. A control loop that waits for a network round trip is too slow for anything reactive. At the speeds involved, a few hundred milliseconds is the difference between avoiding an obstacle and hitting it.

 Bandwidth. Raw sensor data is enormous. Sending it off-platform for analysis is wasteful when it is possible and impossible when it is not.

 Exposure. Every byte leaving the platform is a byte someone can intercept, and every dependency on a remote service is a dependency an adversary can attack.

 The moment a platform is most alone is exactly the moment it most needs to be capable. 

## What it costs to build

 Deciding to run at the edge is easy. Making capable intelligence fit is the hard part, and it is where most of the engineering effort actually goes.

 Onboard compute is bounded by weight, heat and power, and those three are linked. More capable compute is heavier and draws more current, which reduces endurance; it also produces heat, which must be removed, which costs weight again. Every watt spent thinking is a watt not spent moving. On a small platform, that trade is brutal and constant.

 The disciplines that follow are unglamorous but decisive: designing and compressing models to run usefully in a small envelope; guaranteeing the loop completes on schedule every time rather than usually; sustaining performance without thermal throttling; and shedding non-essential work gracefully under load instead of falling over.

## Determinism over peak performance

 There is a temptation to optimise for the best-case number — how fast the model runs when nothing else is competing for the hardware. That figure is close to meaningless in a real system, where perception, navigation, control and communications all contend for the same silicon simultaneously.

 What matters is the worst case: does the loop still close on time when everything is running at once and the platform is hot? A system that is usually fast and occasionally late is, for control purposes, simply unreliable.

## The compounding benefit

 Once a system genuinely does not need the link, several things improve at once. It stays useful when isolated. It decides at sensor rate rather than network rate. It exposes far less. And the bandwidth that does exist can carry conclusions rather than raw data — which is a better use of a scarce resource in any case.

 This is why we settled the architecture early, in 2021, rather than treating it as something to retrofit. Decisions of this kind are extremely expensive to reverse once an entire stack has been built on the opposite assumption.

 — Rewind Dynamics · Perspective 
 Back to Insights

Navigating Without the Sky — GPS-Denied | Rewind Dynamics 

 Skip to content 

 01 Home 
 02 Company 
 03 Systems 
 04 Capabilities 
 05 Applications 
 06 Technology 
 07 Research 
 08 Investors 
 09 Careers 
 10 Newsroom 
 11 Contact 

 Perspective 11 March 2026 New Delhi 

## Navigating without the sky

 Satellite navigation is weak, jammable and spoofable. For an autonomous defence system, assuming it will be there is a design flaw — so we treat its absence as the normal case.

 Satellite navigation is so reliable in daily life that it has become invisible. It is also, from a defence perspective, remarkably fragile — and it is usually the first thing an adversary removes.

 The physics explain why. A satellite positioning signal is transmitted from roughly twenty thousand kilometres away by a modest transmitter. By the time it arrives it is extraordinarily weak — below the background noise. Overwhelming it locally takes very little power.

## Jamming is the lesser problem

 Jamming denies the signal, and a well-designed system notices immediately: the fix is gone, and it can fall back to other methods. Unpleasant, but honest.

 Spoofing is worse. A spoofer transmits a plausible but false signal, and the receiver reports a confident, precise, wrong position. The system does not know anything is amiss. Every decision downstream is then made on a false premise, and the more the platform trusts its navigation, the further astray it goes.

 A system that knows it is lost is manageable. A system confidently reporting the wrong position is dangerous. 

## What replaces it

 There is no single substitute. What works is combining several independent methods with different failure modes, so that the loss of any one degrades the estimate rather than destroying it.

 Visual odometry. Estimating motion by tracking how the scene shifts across the camera between frames. Accurate over short intervals, and dependent on there being something to look at.

 Mapping and relocalisation. Building a map of the surroundings while determining position within it, and recognising places seen before to correct accumulated error.

 Inertial dead reckoning. Carrying the estimate forward using motion sensors. Excellent briefly, drifting steadily, and entirely independent of the outside world.

 Fused estimation. Weighting each source by how much it can currently be trusted — and, critically, tracking how confident the combined estimate deserves to be.

## Managing error, not eliminating it

 Navigation without external reference is fundamentally about error management. Every dead-reckoned estimate drifts; the question is how quickly, and how often you can correct it against something recognisable. This is why featureless environments are so difficult — open water, desert, snow, darkness and smoke all deprive vision of the landmarks it needs.

 Repetitive environments create the opposite failure. A corridor that looks identical to four other corridors invites confident relocalisation to the wrong one, which produces the same dangerous condition as spoofing: precision without accuracy.

## The feature that matters most

 If we had to name a single property that distinguishes a serious navigation stack from a demonstration, it would not be accuracy. It would be knowing how accurate it currently is .

 A system that reports 'my position estimate has degraded and I no longer trust it' has given the operator something actionable. A system that keeps reporting a confident figure as its error grows has given them a trap. We design for the former, and we treat honest uncertainty as a first-class output rather than an afterthought.

## Why we treat denial as normal

 A great many autonomous systems are built assuming satellite navigation is available, with a degraded fallback bolted on afterwards. We invert that: the system is designed to work without it, and treats a satellite fix as a useful corrective when it happens to be available and trustworthy.

 This is more expensive to build. It is also the only version that survives contact with an environment where someone is actively trying to make your system lost.

 — Rewind Dynamics · Perspective 
 Back to Insights

Command, Not Control — Human Authority | Rewind Dynamics 

 Skip to content 

 01 Home 
 02 Company 
 03 Systems 
 04 Capabilities 
 05 Applications 
 06 Technology 
 07 Research 
 08 Investors 
 09 Careers 
 10 Newsroom 
 11 Contact 

 Perspective 18 November 2025 New Delhi 

## Command, not control

 Everyone says a human stays in the loop. Far fewer say what that means in engineering terms — or what happens to the principle when one person is directing many systems at once.

 Almost every organisation building autonomous systems says that a human stays in the loop. The phrase has become so common that it has stopped carrying much information. It is worth being precise about what it can actually mean, because the versions differ enormously in their consequences.

## Three arrangements, often confused

 Human in the loop. The system cannot take a significant action until a person approves it. Maximum control, and it does not scale — the operator becomes the bottleneck, which defeats much of the purpose.

 Human on the loop. The system acts within set limits while a person supervises continuously and can intervene or stop it at any moment.

 Human out of the loop. The system acts without a person available to intervene within the relevant timeframe.

 These are frequently discussed as if they were points on a single dial of trust. They are not. They describe different distributions of responsibility, and the third one is where the serious ethical weight sits.

## Why we say command rather than loop

 Our own framing is deliberately different: a person is always in command . The distinction is not pedantry. 'In the loop' describes a mechanism — where a human sits relative to a decision cycle. 'In command' describes responsibility, which is the thing that actually matters.

 Machines carry out tasks. People set the rules, define the limits, and remain answerable for the outcome. 
 A commander does not personally perform every action taken under their authority. They set the objective, define what is and is not permitted, retain the ability to intervene, and answer for the result. That relationship is well understood in military organisations, and it transfers to autonomous systems more usefully than a diagram about loops.

## What it requires in engineering

 Stating the principle is easy. Building for it changes the architecture in specific ways:

 Bounded discretion. The system operates freely inside limits a person has set, and stops at their edge rather than improvising past it.

 Legible behaviour. An operator must be able to anticipate what the system will do. A system that is brilliant but surprising cannot be commanded, only watched.

 Clean hand-off. Transferring control between autonomy and operator without ambiguity about who currently holds it. Confusion here is a known cause of accidents in every automated domain.

 Recognising its own limits. Knowing when a situation has moved outside what it should handle alone, and escalating rather than continuing.

 Reconstructable decisions. Recording enough that any action can be examined afterwards and explained. Accountability without a record is an aspiration, not a practice.

## Scale is the hard case

 The principle is straightforward with one platform and one operator. It gets harder when a single person directs many systems, which is precisely the situation autonomy is meant to enable.

 Approving every action does not survive contact with numbers. Our position is that command operates at the level of the task and its boundaries: a person sets what is to be achieved and what must not happen, retains the ability to intervene or recall at any point, and remains responsible. The system's job is to make that supervision tractable — reporting clearly, escalating honestly, and never quietly expanding its own remit.

## A commitment, not a feature

 We treat this as a constraint on what we will build rather than an option a customer can configure away. It is stated in our responsible autonomy commitments and it shapes what we agree to work on.

 There is a commercial cost to holding a line like this, and we would rather absorb it than discover later that we built something we cannot defend.

 — Rewind Dynamics · Perspective 
 Back to Insights

Mass, Reimagined — The Economics of Swarms | Rewind Dynamics 

 Skip to content 

 01 Home 
 02 Company 
 03 Systems 
 04 Capabilities 
 05 Applications 
 06 Technology 
 07 Research 
 08 Investors 
 09 Careers 
 10 Newsroom 
 11 Contact 

 Perspective 21 May 2026 New Delhi 

## Mass, reimagined

 Cheap, numerous autonomous systems change what it is reasonable to risk — and therefore what questions a force can afford to ask. But quantity alone is a staffing crisis, not a capability.

 Mass — having more of something than your opponent — is one of the oldest ideas in warfare, and one of the most expensive. For the last several decades, Western defence procurement moved decisively the other way: fewer, more capable, more expensive platforms, each so valuable that losing one is a strategic event.

 Small autonomous systems reopen the question, because they change what a single unit costs and therefore what it is reasonable to risk.

## The exchange rate problem

 The clearest illustration is defensive. If a threat costs very little to produce and the established means of countering it costs a great deal, the defender loses the exchange even when every single engagement succeeds. Win often enough at that rate and you are still bankrupt.

 The same arithmetic applies offensively, and to reconnaissance. If answering a question about a location requires risking an expensive platform, there are questions you simply will not ask. Lower the cost of asking and the set of feasible questions expands dramatically.

 Cheapness is not a compromise on capability. At sufficient scale, it is a different capability. 

## Why 'more drones' is not a swarm

 It is tempting to conclude that the answer is simply quantity. It is not. A hundred platforms each requiring an operator is not mass; it is a staffing crisis. The value only materialises if the group can be directed as a single entity — which is a software problem, and a hard one.

 A genuine swarm has properties that a collection does not:

 Tasking scales sub-linearly. One operator directs the group; workload does not grow with the number of members.

 The picture is shared. What one member observes informs what the others do, producing an understanding none of them had alone.

 Attrition degrades rather than stops. Losing members reduces capability proportionately instead of ending the task.

 Coordination survives poor communication. Members cannot assume a reliable link to each other, let alone to a central controller.

## The two-tier idea

 One architecture we find genuinely interesting is a two-tier arrangement: a larger carrier platform that provides range, endurance, compute and communications, releasing a group of very small platforms to do the close-in work.

 The appeal is the division of labour. The small platforms carry almost nothing but sensing and autonomy, which is precisely why they can go low, close and into spaces a larger aircraft cannot. The carrier stays back, coordinates them, and relays what they find to the people in command. Neither tier could do the job alone.

 We describe this at concept level deliberately. It is a research direction, not a product, and the engineering questions underneath it — coordination on almost no bandwidth, collision avoidance in tight volumes, cost per unit — are exactly the ones that decide whether the idea survives contact with reality.

## The accountability question

 Numbers raise a question that a single platform does not: what does meaningful human command look like when there are many systems rather than one? We do not think the answer is a person approving every action — that reintroduces the workload problem the architecture exists to solve.

 Our position is that command operates at the level of the task and its limits. A person sets what the group is to achieve and the boundaries it must not cross, retains the ability to intervene or recall at any point, and remains responsible for the outcome. That principle does not become negotiable because the system got larger.

## Where this sits

 Mass through small autonomous systems is one of the more consequential shifts in the field, and it is early. Our work here is research: we describe the shape of the idea publicly and keep the engineering for the people who need it.

 — Rewind Dynamics · Perspective

Building the founding engineering team — Rewind Dynamics

 Company 22 March 2021 New Delhi 

## Building the founding engineering team

 Great autonomy comes from great engineers. An update on the team we're assembling and the disciplines we're hiring for.

 A company like ours is only as good as the people who build it. Over the past year our focus has been on assembling a founding engineering team with the range of skills that autonomous systems demand.

## The disciplines it takes

 Autonomy sits at the meeting point of several hard fields, and we're bringing them together under one roof:

 Autonomy and planning — the decision-making core of every system.

 Perception and computer vision — turning sensor data into understanding.

 Robotics and controls — flight, locomotion and stable motion.

 Embedded and edge systems — making it all run on real, constrained hardware.

## How we work

 We keep teams small, ownership high, and the loop between building and testing short. People here own outcomes rather than tickets, and the best idea wins regardless of who has it. We test honestly and let the data decide.

 We're hiring builders — people who would rather make the thing than talk about it. 

## Join us

 The people who join now will shape both the technology and the company. If that appeals to you, take a look at our open roles — or just write to us and tell us where you'd make the biggest difference.

 Perspective 30 September 2021 New Delhi 

## Edge AI: why the intelligence has to live on the platform

 For defence autonomy, running AI on the device rather than in the cloud isn't an optimisation — it's a requirement. Here's how we think about it.

 There's a simple design question at the heart of every autonomous system: where does the thinking happen? For a lot of consumer technology, the answer is “in the cloud.” For defence autonomy, we think the answer has to be “on the platform.”

## The link cannot be assumed

 In the field, communications are contested. Links get jammed, degraded or simply drop. A system that depends on a distant server to make decisions stops being useful the moment that connection fails — which is often exactly when it matters most.

 Running the intelligence on the device itself removes that dependency. The system keeps sensing, deciding and acting whether or not it can talk to anyone.

## Latency and data both argue for the edge

 There are two more reasons. First, latency : round-tripping every decision to a server and back is too slow for something moving through the real world. Second, data : what a system sees can stay on the system, rather than being shipped elsewhere.

 Connectivity should be a bonus, never a crutch. A capable system earns its keep with the link down. 

## What that demands of us

 Edge AI is harder to build. It means designing models and software that run in real time on small, low-power hardware, within tight limits on size, weight and power. That constraint shapes a lot of our engineering — and we think it's the right constraint to design around.

 — Rewind Dynamics · Newsroom
