 Programme 5 August 2026 New Delhi 

## Preparing for our first mission test this December

 Everything we have built so far has lived in development and simulation. This December we plan to put it to its first real-world mission test.

 We want to be plain about where we are. In six years, Rewind Dynamics has not fielded, deployed or proven an autonomous system in the real world. Everything we have built so far lives in development and in simulation. That has been deliberate.

## Why we've taken our time

 Autonomy for defence is not a place to cut corners. We have spent our time on the fundamentals — the autonomy core, perception and the systems engineering underneath — and proving behaviour in software, where a difficult scenario can be repeated a thousand times at no risk. We would rather earn confidence slowly than claim it early.

## What the first mission test is

 This December, for the first time, we plan to take that work out of simulation and into a first end-to-end mission test — an autonomous system attempting a representative task in the real world, start to finish, under our supervision.

 We're calling it what it is: a test. The point is not a polished demonstration; it is to find out honestly what holds up outside the model and what doesn't. Some of it will work. Some of it will send us back to the bench. Both are the job.

 We don't test to prove we're right. We test to find out where we're wrong — while it's still cheap to fix. 

## How we'll go about it

 The approach is the one that has guided us from the start: software-proven first, a human firmly in command throughout, and an honest assessment afterward of what went right, what went wrong, and why. Whatever the outcome, we'll learn from it and feed it straight back into the next iteration.

## Where this leads

 A first mission test is a beginning, not a finish line. It marks the point where our research starts meeting reality — and it's exactly the kind of milestone that partners, evaluators and investors tend to want to follow closely. If that's you, we'd be glad to talk: please get in touch .

 Company 26 January 2020 New Delhi 

## Rewind Dynamics is founded in New Delhi

 We are starting Rewind Dynamics to design and build autonomous systems for defence and military needs.

 Today — on Republic Day — we are formally launching Rewind Dynamics , a defence-technology company based in New Delhi. Our purpose is simple to state and hard to do well: to design and build autonomous systems that are genuinely useful to the people who defend and protect.

## Why we're doing this

 Autonomy is becoming decisive across modern defence. Systems that can sense, decide and act on their own reduce risk to personnel and multiply what a small team can achieve. We believe the forces that depend on these systems should be able to own them — designed and understood in-house, not imported as a black box.

 That belief is the reason Rewind Dynamics exists. We want to contribute real, trustworthy autonomy to the defence and military users who depend on it — wherever in the world they operate.

## What we'll build

 We are focused on three families of autonomous systems:

 Unmanned aerial systems — for surveillance, reconnaissance and force protection.

 Precision guidance — accurate, accountable guidance for defence effects.

 Tactical miniature systems — compact, man-portable autonomy for dismounted use.

 All three sit on a shared core of autonomy, perception and dependable systems engineering.

## How we'll work

 Our name describes our method. We test, we rewind and assess what happened — what went right, what went wrong — and we improve. Dependable autonomy is earned through disciplined engineering and honest testing, not a single flashy demonstration.

 We would rather build carefully and earn trust than over-promise. That is the company we intend to be. 
 We are at the very beginning, and there is a great deal to do. If you are an engineer, a potential partner, or someone in the defence ecosystem who shares this ambition, we would like to hear from you.

 Perspective 24 November 2022 New Delhi 

## Autonomy, with a human always in command

 Autonomy is powerful precisely because it acts on its own — which is exactly why a person must stay in command. How we think about responsible autonomy.

 The most common worry about autonomous systems is also the most reasonable one: if a machine decides for itself, who is responsible? Our answer is simple, and we build around it. A person is always in command. 

## Machines execute; people decide

 An autonomous system can carry out a task without someone steering it moment to moment. That's the point — it's what makes autonomy useful. But carrying out a task and deciding whether it should happen are two different things. The second belongs to people, and our systems are designed to keep it there.

## Guardrails, not guesswork

 In practice that means clear limits on what a system will and won't do, a person able to supervise and intervene at any time, and behaviour that stays inside defined bounds. Autonomy operates on a leash of our choosing — long or short as the task requires.

 Trustworthy autonomy is autonomy you can predict, supervise and switch off. 

## Assessment closes the loop

 Responsibility doesn't end when a run does. We keep records and assess every run honestly — what went right, what went wrong, and why — then feed that back into the design. Accountability you can inspect after the fact is what makes autonomy something an institution can actually adopt.

 This isn't a constraint we tolerate; it's a principle we design toward. It's how autonomy earns its place.

 — Rewind Dynamics · Newsroom

 Perspective 18 August 2020 New Delhi 

## The case for trustworthy autonomy in defence

 Trustworthy autonomy is not a luxury — it is fast becoming a requirement. Our view on why defence forces should be able to own the systems they depend on.

 Every serious defence establishment is investing in autonomy. Uncrewed and autonomous systems are changing how surveillance is done, how forces are protected, and how risk is managed. The question for any force is not whether to adopt them, but whether to own them.

## The problem with importing capability

 Buying finished systems from abroad can be quick, but it comes with quiet costs. You inherit someone else's design choices, you depend on their supply chain and support, and the most important parts — the autonomy and the software — often arrive as a sealed box you cannot fully inspect or adapt.

 For something as consequential as autonomy, that is a poor trade. Capability you cannot understand is capability you cannot truly trust.

## Owned capability is trustworthy capability

 When a system is designed, built and understood in-house, it can be inspected, adapted and maintained on your own terms. It can be tuned for the conditions it actually operates in. And the expertise compounds over time instead of leaving with a vendor.

 Trustworthy autonomy isn't about where a system is made. It's about being able to trust, adapt and improve the systems you depend on. 

## Our part in it

 This is the space Rewind Dynamics is being built to work in. We are focused on autonomy — unmanned aerial, precision-guided and tactical systems — engineered from first principles and owned end to end. It is a long road, and no single company covers all of it, but a healthy field is built one serious team at a time.

 We're glad to be one of them.

 — Rewind Dynamics · Newsroom

 Perspective 18 June 2026 New Delhi 

## Why the tactical edge belongs to autonomy

 Small, autonomous systems change what a dismounted team can see and do. Our view on why the tactical edge is where autonomy earns its keep.

 Big platforms get the attention, but some of the most useful autonomy is small enough to carry. Compact autonomous systems — the kind a soldier can put in a pack — quietly change what a dismounted team can see and do.

## Extending the senses of a small team

 A tactical autonomous system can look around the next corner, watch a route, or hold an eye on an area — without putting a person in the exposed position to do it. That's a meaningful shift in risk and awareness for the people at the sharp end.

## The discipline of small

 Working at this scale is its own engineering discipline. Size, weight and power are all tightly limited, so every capability has to earn its place. Simplicity and ruggedness matter more than features; a system that's fiddly or fragile is worse than no system at all.

 At the tactical edge, dependable and simple beats clever and delicate every time. 

## Where we fit

 Tactical miniature systems are one of the three families we develop, precisely because the constraints are so demanding. Getting capable autonomy into a small, rugged, man-portable package is exactly the kind of hard problem we started Rewind Dynamics to work on.

 To discuss our work in this area, please reach out .

 Programme 16 May 2022 New Delhi 

## Commencing development of our first unmanned aerial system

 A milestone for the team: we have begun focused development on our first autonomous unmanned aerial system.

 We're pleased to share a milestone. After two years building the team and the groundwork, we have begun focused development on our first autonomous unmanned aerial system .

## What we're focused on

 Our emphasis is on the autonomy that makes a UAV genuinely useful in the field, rather than on any single flashy feature. That means:

 Reliable autonomous navigation, with the operator supervising rather than piloting.

 Useful onboard perception — detecting and reporting what matters.

 Sensible behaviour when the link is degraded or the picture is incomplete.

## Software first

 In keeping with how we work, a great deal of this begins in simulation. We prove behaviour in software — where we can repeat difficult situations as often as we like — before committing to hardware and the field.

 We record every run, assess it honestly, and feed what we learn straight back into the next iteration. 

## What's next

 This is the start of a long, careful process, and we'll be deliberate about what we say and when. For partners and evaluators interested in the detail, the right way to engage is directly — please get in touch .
